text: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (DBMS) Comprehensive Theoretical Foundations, Architectural Frameworks, Formal Relational Theory, Normalization, SQL Syntax, and Transaction Processing Document Scope and Theoretical Foundations This document serves as an exhaustive theoretical reference manual for Database Management Systems (DBMS), systematically covering the foundational concepts, system architectures, conceptual data modeling, relational algebra, database design theory, normalization, structured query language (SQL), transaction processing, concurrency control, and modern NoSQL paradigms. All theoretical formulations, keyword definitions, architectural diagrams represented as tables, algorithms, and SQL syntaxes are rigorously grounded in standard university database curricula (BCS403 Modules 1 through 5). Module 1: Introduction to Database Systems & Conceptual Modeling 1.1 Basic Definitions and Database System Concepts Databases and database technology play a pivotal role in modern computer applications, forming the underlying infrastructure for business, electronic commerce, engineering, medicine, education, and research systems. Understanding the core definitions is essential for establishing a formal framework. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Database A database is a logically coherent collection of related data with some inherent meaning, designed, built, and populated with data for a specific purpose, representing some aspect of the real world (sometimes called the Miniworld or Universe of Discourse). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Data refers to known facts that can be recorded and that have implicit meaning. Data represents raw facts prior to contextual interpretation. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Database Management System (DBMS) A DBMS is a general-purpose software system that facilitates the processes of defining, constructing, manipulating, and sharing databases among various users and applications. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Meta-data is descriptive information stored in the DBMS catalog or dictionary that defines the database structure, data types, relationships, format details, and integrity constraints. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Database System A Database System refers to the combination of the database itself, the DBMS software, the hardware infrastructure, and the associated application software.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Database System A Database System refers to the combination of the database itself, the DBMS software, the hardware infrastructure, and the associated application software. 1.2 Characteristics of the Database Approach vs. Traditional File Systems In traditional file processing, each user group designs and implements its own files and application programs. This approach leads to severe limitations, including data redundancy, inconsistency, rigid program-data dependency, and lack of multiuser control. The database approach overcomes these limitations through four fundamental characteristics: Self-Describing Nature of a Database System: A fundamental characteristic of the database approach is that the system contains not only the database itself but also a complete definition or description of the database structure and constraints stored in the system catalog (meta-data). Insulation Between Programs and Data (Program-Data Independence): In traditional file processing, the structure of data files is embedded directly into application code. In a DBMS, file structures and storage formats are managed independently by the catalog. Changing data storage structures does not require altering application programs. Data Abstraction: A DBMS provides users with a conceptual representation of data that hides detailed physical storage specifications. A data model is used to express this abstract representation. Support of Multiple Views of the Data: A database typically has many distinct users, each requiring a customized view or subset of the database. Views can display virtual data derived from stored base relations. Sharing of Data and Multiuser Transaction Processing: A multiuser DBMS allows multiple concurrent users to access and modify the database simultaneously. Concurrency control facilities guarantee that concurrent transactions operate correctly without data corruption (OLTP applications).

Concurrency control facilities guarantee that concurrent transactions operate correctly without data corruption (OLTP applications). 1.3 Database System Users and Roles Database users are broadly categorized into two major categories: 'Actors on the Scene' (those who manage or use the database content) and 'Workers Behind the Scene' (those who build and maintain the DBMS software infrastructure). Category User Role Primary Responsibilities & Characteristics Actors on Scene Database Administrator (DBA) Responsible for authorizing access, monitoring database usage, acquiring software/hardware resources, and overseeing security/performance. Actors on Scene Database Designers Responsible for identifying data to be stored, choosing appropriate structures, and designing conceptual/logical schemas. Actors on Scene Casual End Users Access the database occasionally, requesting different information each time using sophisticated interactive query interfaces. Actors on Scene Naive / Parametric Users Form the main job function; execute pre-written canned transactions (e.g., bank tellers, reservation agents). Actors on Scene Sophisticated End Users Engineers, scientists, and analysts who thoroughly understand DBMS capabilities and implement complex custom applications. Actors on Scene System Analysts & Programmers Determine parametric user requirements and write, debug, test canned application programs. Workers Behind DBMS System Designers Design and implement the internal DBMS modules, compilers, query optimizers, and storage engines. Workers Behind Tool Developers Build software packages (GUI tools, design wizards, performance monitoring tools) that complement the DBms. Workers Behind Operators & Maintenance Handle day-to-day operational execution, server maintenance, backup schedules, and hardware upkeep.

Workers Behind Tool Developers Build software packages (GUI tools, design wizards, performance monitoring tools) that complement the DBms. Workers Behind Operators & Maintenance Handle day-to-day operational execution, server maintenance, backup schedules, and hardware upkeep. 1.4 Advantages and Disadvantages of Using a DBMS The database approach provides vast improvements over file-processing, including: (1) Controlling data redundancy through normalization, (2) Restricting unauthorized access via security sub-systems, (3) Providing persistent storage for program objects, (4) Providing efficient query processing using indexes and tree structures, (5) Providing backup and recovery services, and (6) Enforcing complex integrity constraints. Conversely, a DBMS may involve unnecessary overhead when a database is very simple, single-user, subject to stringent real-time constraints, or when the high initial investment in software, hardware, and training cannot be justified. 1.5 Three-Schema Architecture and Data Independence The goal of the three-schema architecture is to separate user applications from the physical database. It defines three distinct levels: KEYWORD DEFINITION: Internal Schema (Internal Level) Describes the physical storage structure of the database using a physical data model. Details physical access paths, block storage, indexing, and data compression. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Conceptual Schema (Conceptual Level) Describes the structure of the entire database for a community of users, hiding physical storage details. Focuses on entities, data types, relationships, user operations, and constraints. KEYWORD DEFINITION: External Schema (External/View Level) Describes the specific user views or subsets of the database relevant to specific user groups. The process of transforming requests and results between levels is called mapping. The three-schema architecture supports two forms of Data Independence: Logical Data Independence: The capacity to change the conceptual schema without having to change external schemas or application programs. Physical Data Independence: The capacity to change the internal schema without having to change the conceptual schema (or external schemas).

1.6 DBMS Component Modules and Internal Architecture Modern DBMS packages are modular systems consisting of several specialized software components: DDL Compiler: Processes schema definitions specified in DDL and stores metadata descriptions in the catalog. Interactive Query Interface & Compiler: Parses, verifies, and compiles high-level queries (SQL) entered interactively. Query Optimizer: Rearranges and transforms query operations to establish an optimal execution plan. Runtime Database Processor: Executes compiled queries and transactions, interacting directly with the stored data manager. Stored Data Manager / Buffer Manager: Controls access to DBMS information stored on disk, managing main memory RAM buffering and page caching. 1.7 Conceptual Data Modeling using the Entity-Relationship (ER) Model The Entity-Relationship (ER) model is a high-level conceptual data model used to construct a detailed representation of an organization's data independently of software or hardware constraints. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Entity A thing or object in the real world with an independent existence that can be uniquely identified (e.g., a specific Employee, Course, or Car). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Entity Type A collection or set of entities that share the same attributes (e.g., the EMPLOYEE entity type). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Attribute A particular property or characteristic that describes an entity. Classification of Attributes in ER Modeling Simple (Atomic) Attributes: Attributes that are not divisible into smaller components (e.g., SSN, Age). Composite Attributes: Attributes that can be divided into smaller subparts with independent meanings (e.g., Address divided into Street, City, State, Zip). Single-Valued Attributes: Attributes that hold a single atomic value for a particular entity (e.g., Birth_Date). Multi-Valued Attributes: Attributes that can have a set of values for the same entity (e.g., College_Degrees, Phone_Numbers). Represented as double ovals. Derived Attributes: Attributes whose value is calculated or derived from another attribute (e.g., Age derived from Birth_Date). Represented as dashed ovals.

Multi-Valued Attributes: Attributes that can have a set of values for the same entity (e.g., College_Degrees, Phone_Numbers). Represented as double ovals. Derived Attributes: Attributes whose value is calculated or derived from another attribute (e.g., Age derived from Birth_Date). Represented as dashed ovals. Key Attribute: An attribute whose values are distinct and unique for each individual entity in an entity set (e.g., Student_Number). Underlined in ER diagrams. Relationships and Structural Constraints KEYWORD DEFINITION: Relationship Type A structural association among two or more participating entity types. The degree of a relationship refers to the number of participating entity types (Binary = 2, Ternary = 3). Structural constraints constrain the possible combinations of entities that can participate in a relationship set: Cardinality Ratio: Specifies the maximum number of relationship instances that an entity can participate in (1:1, 1:N, N:1, or N:M). Participation Constraint: Specifies whether the existence of an entity depends on its being related to another entity via the relationship type. Total Participation (Existence Dependency) requires every entity to participate (double line). Partial Participation allows entities to exist without participating (single line). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Weak Entity Type An entity type that does not possess sufficient key attributes to be uniquely identified on its own. A weak entity type must participate in a total identifying relationship with an owner entity type and is identified using a Partial Key (Discriminator). Module 2: Relational Data Model, Relational Algebra & ER Mapping 2.1 Relational Model Concepts and Terminology The relational model represents a database as a collection of relations (tables). Formally, a relation is a mathematical set of tuples (rows), underpinned by first-order predicate logic and set theory. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Relation Schema Denoted by R(A1, A2, ..., An), consisting of a relation name R and a list of attributes A1..An defining the structure.

Formally, a relation is a mathematical set of tuples (rows), underpinned by first-order predicate logic and set theory. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Relation Schema Denoted by R(A1, A2, ..., An), consisting of a relation name R and a list of attributes A1..An defining the structure. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Relation State Denoted by r(R), a set of n-tuples r = {t1, t2, ..., tm}, where each tuple t is an ordered list of n values t = <v1, v2, ..., vn>. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Domain A set of atomic, indivisible values representing the allowable range of data for an attribute. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Degree of a Relation The total number of attributes (columns) in its relation schema. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Cardinality of a Relation The total number of tuples (rows) present in the current relation state. 2.2 Relational Integrity Constraints Integrity constraints are conditions that must hold true for all valid database states. They are classified into four core types: Domain Constraint: Specifies that within each tuple, the value of each attribute A must be an atomic value drawn from the domain dom(A). Key Constraints & Superkeys: A Superkey SK is a set of attributes such that no two distinct tuples in any valid relation state r(R) have the same value for SK. A Candidate Key K is a minimal superkey (removal of any attribute destroys uniqueness). The Primary Key is the candidate key designated to uniquely identify tuples. Entity Integrity Constraint: States that no primary key value can be NULL in any tuple of a base relation, because primary keys are used to identify individual tuples. Referential Integrity Constraint: A constraint specified between two relations (referencing relation R1 and referenced relation R2).

Entity Integrity Constraint: States that no primary key value can be NULL in any tuple of a base relation, because primary keys are used to identify individual tuples. Referential Integrity Constraint: A constraint specified between two relations (referencing relation R1 and referenced relation R2). A foreign key FK in R1 references primary key PK of R2 such that for every tuple in R1, the FK value must either match a PK value in R2 or be NULL. 2.3 Relational Algebra Operations Relational Algebra is a formal procedural query language consisting of operations that take one or two relations as input and produce a new relation as output. Operations are grouped into Unary and Binary categories. Operation Symbol Type / Inputs Formal Definition & Description SELECT σ_condition(R) Unary (1 Relation) Filters tuples from R that satisfy the logical selection condition. Commutative. PROJECT π_attr_list(R) Unary (1 Relation) Selects specified columns from R and eliminates duplicate tuples automatically. RENAME ρ_S(B1..Bn)(R) Unary (1 Relation) Renames the relation schema to S and attribute names to B1..Bn. UNION R ∪ S Binary (Union Compatible) Returns all tuples present in R, S, or both. Duplicate tuples are eliminated. INTERSECTION R ∩ S Binary (Union Compatible) Returns tuples that appear in both R and S relations simultaneously. SET DIFFERENCE R - S Binary (Union Compatible) Returns tuples present in relation R but NOT present in relation S. R × S Binary (Any 2 Relations) Combines every tuple of R with every tuple of S. Degree = n+m, Cardinality = n*m. CARTESIAN PRODUCT EQUIJOIN R ⋈_cond S Binary (Any 2 Relations) Theta join where condition uses strictly equality comparisons (=). NATURAL JOIN R ⋈ S Binary (Shared Attributes) Equijoin on all common attribute names, automatically stripping redundant duplicate columns.

Degree = n+m, Cardinality = n*m. CARTESIAN PRODUCT EQUIJOIN R ⋈_cond S Binary (Any 2 Relations) Theta join where condition uses strictly equality comparisons (=). NATURAL JOIN R ⋈ S Binary (Shared Attributes) Equijoin on all common attribute names, automatically stripping redundant duplicate columns. DIVISION R ÷ S Binary (Attribute Subset) Returns tuples in R that match with ALL tuples present in relation S. 2.4 ER-to-Relational Mapping Algorithm Mapping a conceptual ER diagram into a relational schema follows a systematic 7-step algorithm: Step 1: Mapping Regular Entity Types: For each strong entity type E, create a relation R that includes all simple attributes of E. Choose one key attribute as Primary Key. Step 2: Mapping Weak Entity Types: For each weak entity type W with owner E, create a relation R. Include all simple attributes of W plus the Primary Key of E as a Foreign Key. The composite PK of R is {Owner PK + Partial Key}. Step 3: Mapping Binary 1:1 Relationship Types: Identify relations S and T corresponding to participating entity types. Include PK of S as Foreign Key in T. (Best to choose entity type with total participation for T). Step 4: Mapping Binary 1:N Relationship Types: For each 1:N relationship type, identify relation S (1-side) and T (N-side). Include Primary Key of S as Foreign Key in T. Step 5: Mapping Binary N:M Relationship Types: For each N:M relationship type, create a new lookup relation (cross-reference relation) R. Include PKs of both participating entity types as Foreign Keys in R. Their combination forms the Primary Key of R. Step 6: Mapping Multivalued Attributes: For each multivalued attribute A, create a new relation R. Include attribute A plus the Primary Key of the owner entity as Foreign Key. PK of R is {Owner PK + A}.

Their combination forms the Primary Key of R. Step 6: Mapping Multivalued Attributes: For each multivalued attribute A, create a new relation R. Include attribute A plus the Primary Key of the owner entity as Foreign Key. PK of R is {Owner PK + A}. Step 7: Mapping N-ary Relationship Types: For each n-ary relationship type (degree > 2), create a new relation R. Include PKs of all participating entity types as Foreign Keys. Their combination forms the Primary Key. Module 3: Database Design Theory & Relational Normalization 3.1 Informal Design Guidelines for Relation Schemas Before applying formal normalization algorithms, database designers evaluate schemas using four informal quality guidelines: Guideline 1 (Attribute Semantics): Design relation schemas so that their meaning is easy to explain. Do not combine attributes from multiple entity types into a single relation. Guideline 2 (Redundant Information & Anomalies): Design base relations such that no insertion, deletion, or modification anomalies occur. Redundant storage wastes disk space and risks data inconsistency. Guideline 3 (Reducing NULL Values): Avoid placing attributes in base relations whose values may frequently be NULL. NULL values waste space and cause complex three-valued logic in queries. Guideline 4 (Prohibiting Spurious Tuples): Design relation schemas so that they can be joined on primary/foreign keys without generating spurious (fake) tuples. Decompositions must satisfy the Lossless Join property. 3.2 Update Anomalies KEYWORD DEFINITION: Insertion Anomaly Occurs when inserting a new record requires inserting unneeded or redundant details of another entity, or when data cannot be inserted because primary key values are unavailable. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Deletion Anomaly Occurs when deleting a tuple causes unintended loss of essential data pertaining to a completely different entity. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Modification Anomaly Occurs when updating an attribute value requires updating multiple tuples across the database. Failing to update all tuples creates data inconsistency.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Modification Anomaly Occurs when updating an attribute value requires updating multiple tuples across the database. Failing to update all tuples creates data inconsistency. 3.3 Functional Dependencies (FDs) and Armstrong's Axioms KEYWORD DEFINITION: Functional Dependency (FD) A constraint between two sets of attributes X and Y (denoted X -> Y) specifying that the values of X uniquely determine the values of Y in every valid state r(R). X is called the Determinant. Armstrong's Axioms are sound and complete inference rules used to derive all functional dependencies implied by a set of FDs (F): Reflexive Rule: If Y is a subset of X, then X -> Y holds. Augmentation Rule: If X -> Y holds, then {X, Z} -> {Y, Z} holds for any attribute set Z. Transitive Rule: If X -> Y and Y -> Z hold, then X -> Z holds. Decomposition Rule (Secondary): If X -> {Y, Z} holds, then X -> Y and X -> Z hold. Union Rule (Secondary): If X -> Y and X -> Z hold, then X -> {Y, Z} holds. Pseudotransitive Rule (Secondary): If X -> Y and {W, Y} -> Z hold, then {W, X} -> Z holds. 3.4 Relational Normal Forms (1NF through 5NF) Normalization is a systematic formal process of analyzing relation schemas based on their functional dependencies and primary keys to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies. Normal Form Core Requirement / Condition Violation Remedy & Decomposition Strategy 1NF All attribute values must be atomic. No repeating groups or nested relations. Remove multi-valued attributes / nested tables into separate relations with owner primary key. 2NF In 1NF and every non-prime attribute is FULLY functionally dependent on the primary key. Eliminate partial key dependencies (X -> Y where X is proper subset of candidate key) into separate tables.

2NF In 1NF and every non-prime attribute is FULLY functionally dependent on the primary key. Eliminate partial key dependencies (X -> Y where X is proper subset of candidate key) into separate tables. 3NF In 2NF and NO non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key. Eliminate transitive dependencies (X -> Y where neither X is key nor Y is prime attribute). BCNF Strict 3NF: For every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X MUST be a Superkey. Decompose relation R into {X ∪ Y} and {R - Y} whenever X is not a superkey. 4NF In BCNF and contains no nontrivial Multivalued Dependencies (X ↠ Y). Decompose relation R into {X ∪ Y} and {R - Y} to isolate independent multivalued facts. 5NF (PJNF) In 4NF and contains no nontrivial Join Dependencies (JD) not implied by candidate keys. Decompose relation into 3 or more projections to satisfy non-loss join requirements. 3.5 Properties of Decompositions Non-Additive (Lossless) Join Property: Guarantees that joining the decomposed relations produces exact original tuples without generating spurious tuples. Dependency Preservation Property: Guarantees that all functional dependencies in F can be enforced within individual decomposed relations without requiring join operations. Module 4: Structured Query Language (SQL) & Transaction Concepts 4.1 SQL Schema Definition and Constraint Specification SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard comprehensive database language used for data definition (DDL), data manipulation (DML), and view/constraint specification. CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT ( Dname VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL UNIQUE, Dnumber INT NOT NULL, Mgr_ssn CHAR(9) NOT NULL, Mgr_start_date DATE, PRIMARY KEY (Dnumber), FOREIGN KEY (Mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn) ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE 4.2 Comparisons Involving NULL and Three-Valued Logic SQL uses Three-Valued Logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN) to handle NULL values. When NULL is compared using arithmetic operators, the result is UNKNOWN.

When NULL is compared using arithmetic operators, the result is UNKNOWN. Operator TRUE & UNKNOWN FALSE & UNKNOWN & UNKNOWN AND UNKNOWN FALSE UNKNOWN OR TRUE UNKNOWN NOT TRUE = FALSE NOT FALSE = TRUE NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN 4.3 Advanced SQL Retrieval Constructs Advanced queries combine aggregate functions (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`), grouping clauses (`GROUP BY`, `HAVING`), subqueries (`IN`, `EXISTS`, `ALL`, `ANY`), and explicit joins. -- Retrieve departments with more than 5 employees and average salary > $50,000 SELECT Dno, COUNT(*), AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 AND AVG(Salary) > 50000; -- Correlated Subquery using EXISTS SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname FROM EMPLOYEE E WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM DEPENDENT D WHERE E.Ssn = D.Essn AND E.Sex = D.Sex 4.4 Views, Assertions, and Triggers KEYWORD DEFINITION: Database View A virtual table defined via a SQL query (`CREATE VIEW`). Views do not physically store data; queries against views are dynamically expanded into queries on underlying base tables. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Assertion A declarative schema-level constraint created using `CREATE ASSERTION` that guarantees business rules spanning multiple tables. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Trigger A procedural statement executed automatically by the DBMS in response to specific data modification events (`BEFORE`/`AFTER` `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`). 4.5 Concurrency Problems in Transaction Processing When transactions execute concurrently without proper isolation, three classic data anomaly problems arise: 1. Lost Update Problem: Occurs when two transactions access the same item and their operations interleave such that one transaction overwrites the update made by the other, losing the change. 2. Dirty Read (Uncommitted Dependency) Problem: Occurs when one transaction updates an item and then fails/aborts, but a second transaction reads the updated value before it is rolled back. 3.

Dirty Read (Uncommitted Dependency) Problem: Occurs when one transaction updates an item and then fails/aborts, but a second transaction reads the updated value before it is rolled back. 3. Incorrect Summary / Unrepeatable Read Problem: Occurs when one transaction calculates an aggregate summary over several items while another transaction updates some of those items during the calculation. Module 5: Transaction Processing, Concurrency Control & NoSQL 5.1 Transaction States and ACID Properties KEYWORD DEFINITION: Transaction A logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations (read, write, update, delete). To ensure database reliability and integrity, the DBMS must preserve four fundamental ACID properties: ACID Property Formal Definition & Meaning Enforcing DBMS Subsystem Atomicity 'All or Nothing' property. A transaction is treated as a single indivisible unit of work; either all operations execute or none. Recovery Manager (Log / Undo buffer) Consistency Preservation property. A transaction must transform the database from one valid consistent state to another valid state. Application Programmers & DBMS Constraint Enforcer Isolation Execution isolation. Concurrent transactions must execute as if each were running independently in isolation. Concurrency Control Subsystem (Lock Manager) Durability Permanence property. Once a transaction commits, its updates persist permanently in storage even after system crashes. Recovery Manager (Redo log / Flush to disk) 5.2 Serializability and Concurrency Control Protocols KEYWORD DEFINITION: Conflict Serializability A schedule S is conflict serializable if it is conflict equivalent to a serial schedule S'. Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a write_item operation. Conflict serializability is verified using a Precedence Graph (Serialization Graph): a directed graph G = (V, E) where nodes represent transactions and directed edges (Ti -> Tj) represent conflicting operations. If the graph contains NO cycles, the schedule is Conflict Serializable.

Conflict serializability is verified using a Precedence Graph (Serialization Graph): a directed graph G = (V, E) where nodes represent transactions and directed edges (Ti -> Tj) represent conflicting operations. If the graph contains NO cycles, the schedule is Conflict Serializable. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol KEYWORD DEFINITION: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) A protocol requiring every transaction to lock/unlock items in two distinct phases: (1) Growing Phase (acquiring locks, no unlocking permitted), and (2) Shrinking Phase (releasing locks, no acquiring permitted). 2PL guarantees conflict serializability. Strict 2PL: Requires that a transaction cannot release any Exclusive (write) locks until after it commits or aborts. Eliminates cascading aborts. Rigorous 2PL: Requires that ALL locks (shared and exclusive) held by a transaction must be retained until the transaction commits or aborts. 5.3 Deadlock and Starvation Handling Deadlock Prevention (Timestamp Protocols): Wait-Die Scheme (Non-preemptive: if older T requests item held by younger T, older T waits; if younger T requests item held by older, younger dies). Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive: if older T requests item held by younger T, older wounds/preempts younger; if younger requests older, younger waits). Deadlock Detection & Recovery: Maintains a Wait-For Graph (WFG). Cycles indicate deadlocks. Recovery involves selecting a victim transaction, rolling it back, and aborting. 5.4 Introduction to NoSQL Database Architectures NoSQL ('Not Only SQL') systems emerged to fulfill requirements of web-scale applications handling massive volumes of unstructured/semi-structured data with high velocity and horizontal scalability requirements. KEYWORD DEFINITION: CAP Theorem States that any distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most TWO of three guarantees: Consistency (C), Availability (A), and Partition Tolerance (P). KEYWORD DEFINITION: BASE Properties Alternative to ACID for distributed systems: Basically Available (system remains accessible), Soft-state (state can change without user input due to eventual consistency), and Eventual consistency.

Internet of Things (IoT) Theory & Concepts Guide A Comprehensive Reference on Architectures, Protocols, Management, Design Methodology, Python Logic, Hardware Endpoints, Cloud Integration, and Big Data Analytics Document Scope & Context This document consolidates comprehensive theoretical fundamentals across the selected chapters. All header/footer artifacts, watermarks, and raw slide image graphics from the source slides have been stripped, presenting pure, structured academic content with explicit keyword definitions and thorough explanations. Chapter 1: Introduction to Internet of Things (IoT) 1.1 Core Definition and System Characteristics The Internet of Things represents a fundamental paradigm shift in hyper-connectivity, bridging physical entities with virtual digital infrastructure across global networks. ▪ Internet of Things (IoT): A dynamic global network infrastructure with self-configuring capabilities based on standard and interoperable communication protocols where physical and virtual 'things' have identities, physical attributes, virtual personalities, intelligent interfaces, and are seamlessly integrated into the information network. ▪ Dynamic & Self-Adapting: The capability of IoT devices and systems to dynamically adapt to changing contexts, operating conditions, user inputs, or environmental parameters (e.g., adaptive video streaming quality based on fluctuating bandwidth). ▪ Self-Configuring: The ability of IoT devices to automatically configure themselves, fetch software updates, discover neighboring nodes, and establish network connectivity without manual human intervention. ▪ Interoperable Communication Protocols: Standardized communication specifications enabling heterogeneous physical devices from different manufacturers to communicate seamlessly across networks. ▪ Unique Identity: The property wherein every physical object or IoT node possesses a distinct identifier (such as an IP address, MAC address, or URI) enabling individual addressing, tracking, and remote control.

1.2 Physical Design of IoT Devices and Hardware Interfaces The physical design of an IoT system centers on the hardware architecture of the 'Things'—the physical endpoints that collect environmental data and perform physical actions. ▪ IoT Device: A physical hardware node equipped with unique identification, sensing, actuation, processing, and communication capabilities that interacts directly or indirectly with external applications or cloud back-ends. ▪ I/O Interfaces: Hardware interface pins (e.g., UART, SPI, I2C, CAN, GPIO) enabling direct physical connection and communication between the central microcontroller/processor and external sensors or actuators. ▪ Connectivity Interfaces: Hardware modules supporting wired or wireless network protocol connection (e.g., USB Host, Ethernet RJ45, Wi-Fi 802.11, Cellular 2G/3G/4G). ▪ Memory & Storage Interfaces: On-board memory units including flash storage (NAND/NOR), external storage (SD/MMC/SDIO), and RAM (DDR1/DDR2/DDR3) used for local data buffering and execution. 1.3 Logical Design and Functional Blocks Logical design provides an abstract, high-level representation of the functional entities and processes composing an IoT system, independent of specific low-level hardware or software implementations. ▪ Logical Design: An abstract structural model detailing system entities, functional capabilities, communication models, and APIs without detailing vendor-specific hardware or software implementations. ▪ Functional Block: A modular architectural component providing specific system capabilities required for identification, sensing, actuation, communication, management, security, or application interface. Device Block: Provides hardware capabilities for remote sensing, actuation, environmental monitoring, and localized control. Communication Block: Manages underlying communication protocols and network interfaces to handle data transmission across nodes. Services Block: Provides essential operational services including device control, data publishing, resource monitoring, and web service endpoints. Management Block: Offers functional tools to configure, monitor, update, and manage the health and operational status of the IoT system. Security Block: Secures the system through user/device authentication, authorization, data encryption, message integrity, and key management.

Management Block: Offers functional tools to configure, monitor, update, and manage the health and operational status of the IoT system. Security Block: Secures the system through user/device authentication, authorization, data encryption, message integrity, and key management. Application Block: The user-facing interface allowing operators to monitor system states, visualize analytics, and send control commands. 1.4 IoT Communication Models IoT systems employ four foundational communication interaction patterns depending on connection latency, decoupling requirements, and messaging topology. ▪ Request-Response Model: A communication model in which a client sends a request to a server, and the server processes the request, retrieves requested resources, and returns an explicit response over a temporary connection. ▪ Publish-Subscribe Model: A decoupled messaging model involving Publishers, Consumers, and a Central Broker. Publishers send data tagged with specific topics to the broker without knowing who the consumers are; the broker forwards messages to all consumers subscribed to those topics. ▪ Push-Pull Model: A queue-based communication pattern in which data producers push messages into shared message queues, and consumers pull messages from the queue. Queues decouple producers/consumers and buffer rate mismatches. ▪ Exclusive Pair Model: A bi-directional, fully duplex communication model utilizing a single persistent connection between client and server, allowing both peers to push messages to each other at any time until explicitly closed. 1.5 Communication APIs and Web Services ▪ REST (Representational State Transfer): An architectural style for designing web services based on stateless request-response communication, focusing on addressing system resources via URIs and manipulating states using standard HTTP commands (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). ▪ WebSocket API: An API providing full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single persistent TCP connection following the Exclusive Pair model, eliminating HTTP header overhead after an initial HTTP handshake.

1.6 Protocol Stack Layers Protocol Layer Supported Standards & Protocols Primary Function in IoT Link Layer 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 WiFi, 802.16 WiMax, 802.15.4 LR-WPAN, 2G/3G/4G Handles physical data transmission and medium access control. Network Layer IPv4, IPv6, 6LoWPAN Provides global node addressing and packet routing across networks. Transport Layer TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol) Offers end-to-end transport (reliable stream vs. low-overhead datagrams). Application Layer HTTP, CoAP, MQTT, XMPP, DDS, AMQP Defines application-level data formatting, RPCs, and messaging paradigms. 1.7 IoT Deployment Levels (Level 1 to Level 6) IoT applications vary significantly in data volume, analysis complexity, and node count. Pacheco & Bahga categorize these into six deployment levels: IoT Level-1: Consists of a single local node that performs sensing/actuation, stores data locally, performs analysis locally, and hosts the application. Ideal for low-cost, low-complexity solutions with small data. IoT Level-2: Features a single node performing sensing/actuation and local analysis. Data is stored in the cloud, and the application is cloud-based. Suitable for big data where primary analysis is computationally light. IoT Level-3: A single node performs sensing/actuation, but data storage, intensive analytics, and applications reside entirely in the cloud. Suited for computationally heavy cloud analysis. IoT Level-4: Features multiple local nodes performing local analysis. Data is sent to the cloud for storage and aggregated cloud applications. Observer nodes subscribe to cloud data streams. IoT Level-5: Comprises multiple end nodes (sensing/actuation) and a central Coordinator Node. The coordinator collects local data and forwards it to the cloud for storage and intensive analysis. Typical for Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs). IoT Level-6: Utilizes multiple independent end nodes sending data to cloud storage. Cloud analytics evaluate big data and trigger control actions via a Centralized Controller node that manages endnode status.

Typical for Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs). IoT Level-6: Utilizes multiple independent end nodes sending data to cloud storage. Chapter 2: Machine-to-Machine (M2M) and Advanced Networking (SDN & NFV) 2.1 Machine-to-Machine (M2M) Framework Machine-to-Machine (M2M) refers to direct point-to-point communication between devices over wired or wireless networks without human intervention. ▪ Machine-to-Machine (M2M): Direct communication between machines or industrial equipment for remote monitoring, status telemetry, and automated control using dedicated local area protocols. ▪ M2M Area Network: A localized network comprising homogeneous machines (M2M nodes) using specialized local protocols such as ZigBee, Bluetooth, ModBus, M-Bus, Wireless M-Bus, or PLC. ▪ M2M Gateway: An intermediary gateway node that performs protocol translation, proxying, and virtual node abstraction to connect non-IP M2M area networks to external IP-based communication networks. ▪ M2M Node: An individual physical device or machine embedded with hardware sensing, actuation, and short-range communication modules within an M2M area network. 2.2 Comparative Analysis: IoT vs. M2M Architectural Dimension Machine-to-Machine (M2M) Internet of Things (IoT) Communication Protocols Proprietary, non-IP or local area protocols (ModBus, ZigBee) in local area. Standardized open IP protocols (IPv6, 6LoWPAN, MQTT, HTTP) end-to-end. Node Heterogeneity Homogeneous devices within isolated point solutions. Highly heterogeneous physical 'Things' with unique virtual identities. Hardware vs. Software Emphasis heavily placed on embedded hardware modules. Emphasis placed on cloud software, microservices, and web APIs. Data Storage & Analysis Data collected in on-premises storage and local point solutions. Data aggregated in public, private, or hybrid cloud for big data analytics. System Integration Isolated vertical silos with local diagnostic applications. Horizontal integration across enterprise cloud apps and global web services. 2.3 Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for IoT Traditional static networks struggle with the dynamic scaling requirements of massive IoT deployments.

System Integration Isolated vertical silos with local diagnostic applications. Horizontal integration across enterprise cloud apps and global web services. 2.3 Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for IoT Traditional static networks struggle with the dynamic scaling requirements of massive IoT deployments. SDN addresses this by decoupling management logic from hardware forwarding. ▪ Software-Defined Networking (SDN): A modern networking architecture that separates the control plane from the data plane and centralizes network intelligence in a programmable software controller. ▪ Control Plane: The software-based decision-making layer in SDN that maintains a global network view, computes routing tables, and manages network policy enforcement. ▪ Data Plane: The underlying infrastructure layer consisting of simple packet-forwarding hardware (switches/routers) that execute packet switching based on control plane rules. ▪ Centralized Network Controller: A central software controller maintaining a unified, global view of the network state, simplifying configuration, provisioning, and traffic engineering. ▪ Northbound Open API: Programmable open APIs used by network management applications to communicate policy requirements down to the SDN control layer. ▪ Southbound Interface (OpenFlow): A standardized communication interface (such as OpenFlow defined by ONF) connecting the central controller to underlying data plane packet-forwarding hardware. 2.4 Network Function Virtualization (NFV) ▪ Network Function Virtualization (NFV): A technology that leverages virtualization to consolidate heterogeneous proprietary network hardware devices onto industry-standard high-volume servers, switches, and storage. ▪ Virtualized Network Function (VNF): A software implementation of a specific network function (e.g., virtual firewall, router, DNS, virtual Home Gateway) capable of running over virtualized infrastructure. ▪ NFV Infrastructure (NFVI): The total hardware (compute, storage, network) and virtualization layer that underpins and executes VNFs. ▪ NFV Management & Orchestration (MANO): The management framework responsible for orchestrating virtualized infrastructure, allocating hardware resources, and managing the lifecycle of VNFs.

Chapter 3: IoT Systems Management with NETCONF and YANG 3.1 Modern Requirements for IoT Systems Management As IoT networks expand to thousands of remote nodes, automated systems management becomes mandatory. Core operator requirements include automated configuration distribution, separation of state data from configuration data, transactional rollbacks, configuration deltas, and role-based access control. 3.2 Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and Its Limitations ▪ Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP): A legacy network management protocol allowing monitoring and basic configuration of network devices via a Network Management Station (NMS), Managed Device, MIB, and SNMP Agent. ▪ Management Information Base (MIB): A hierarchical database structure on a managed device containing variables (objects) representing device operational states or settings. Limitations of SNMP in IoT Networks: Stateless & Unreliable Transport: SNMP operates primarily over UDP without native transport reliability or request acknowledgments. Lack of Writable MIBs: Most vendor MIBs contain read-only operational counters, preventing robust remote configuration changes. No Configuration vs. State Separation: SNMP mixes dynamic operational data with static administrative configuration, making backups difficult. Lack of Transactional Support: SNMP cannot execute multi-device configuration transactions or atomic rollbacks upon failure. 3.3 Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) Architecture ▪ NETCONF: An IETF session-based network management protocol that enables network operators to securely retrieve, edit, copy, and delete configuration data on remote devices using XML-encoded RPCs over SSH. ▪ Configuration Datastore: A distinct conceptual database on a managed device containing valid configuration settings required to bring the device into an operational state. Operations Layer <get-config>, <edit-config>, <copyconfig>, <delete-config>, <lock> Executes explicit operations against configuration datastores. RPC Layer <rpc>, <rpc-reply>, <rpc-error> Provides XML framing for request parameters and server responses.

Transport Layer SSH (Secure Shell), TLS, Console Ensures encrypted, reliable, connectionoriented session framing. 3.4 YANG Data Modeling Language ▪ YANG: A data modeling language used to model configuration data, operational state data, Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs), and notifications manipulated by NETCONF. ▪ Leaf Node: A YANG construct containing a single primitive value (e.g., string, integer, boolean) with no child nodes. ▪ Leaf-List: A YANG construct containing a sequence of primitive values of a specified type (an array of leaves). ▪ Container: A YANG organizational node used to group related child nodes into a named sub-tree structure. ▪ List: A YANG construct representing a sequence of list entries, where each entry acts like a container uniquely identified by one or more key leaves. ▪ YANG Module: A self-contained file containing definitions of data structures, RPC calls, and notification schemas that define the data exchanged between a NETCONF client and server. Step 3: Domain Model Specification: Defines abstract domain entities, physical entities, virtual entities, devices, resources, and services, laying out relationships without technology binding. The Hadoop ecosystem includes HDFS, MapReduce, YARN, HBase (NoSQL database), Zookeeper (coordination), Hive (SQL queries), Pig (dataflow processing), Flume/Sqoop (data ingestion), and Oozie (workflow management). 8.2 Hadoop 1.x Architecture ▪ NameNode: The master node in HDFS that maintains the file system directory tree, file metadata, and block locations across the cluster (a single point of failure in 1.x). ▪ Secondary NameNode: A backup node that periodically merges the NameNode edit logs with the namespace image to create checkpoints. ▪ DataNode: Slave nodes in HDFS that store actual data blocks and serve read/write requests from clients. ▪ JobTracker: The central master service in Hadoop 1.x that assigns MapReduce tasks to specific TaskTracker nodes near data locations. ▪ TaskTracker: Slave node daemons that accept Map, Reduce, and Shuffle tasks from the JobTracker, executing them in spawned JVM processes. 8.3 MapReduce Execution Phases and Heartbeat Mechanism A MapReduce job splits into Map, optional Combine, and Reduce phases. TaskTrackers continuously transmit periodic Heartbeat messages to the JobTracker to verify health and report available task execution slots.

Consists of the Scheduler (enforces resource policies) and ApplicationsManager (AsM, manages ApplicationMaster lifecycles). ▪ ApplicationMaster (AM): A per-application master framework that negotiates resource containers from the RM and coordinates task execution with NodeManagers. ▪ NodeManager (NM): A per-machine slave agent monitoring local container resource utilization and user execution processes. ▪ Container: A logical bundle of physical resources (RAM, CPU cores, network) allocated by the ResourceManager for executing application tasks. 8.5 Hadoop Cluster Scheduling Policies Scheduler Name Allocation Strategy & Logic Best Use Cases & Characteristics FIFO Scheduler Oldest job first in simple submission queue order. Default scheduler; lacks job priority or multi-user fairness. Fair Scheduler Allocates resources equally among all active jobs over time. Organizes jobs into pools with capacity guarantees and deficit tracking. Capacity Scheduler Allocates resources into dedicated, configurable named queues. Operating Systems: Theoretical Principles and Concepts Comprehensive Course Reference Manual (Modules 1 – 5) Module 1: Introduction to Operating Systems, System Structures & Process Concept 1.1 Operating System Fundamentals & Computer Architecture An Operating System (OS) acts as an intermediary between computer user applications and system hardware. It manages system resources, executes user applications, provides an environment for user software development, and enforces protection and security. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Operating System (OS) [Module 1 - Architecture] A foundational software layer that manages computer hardware, system memory, storage, and peripheral devices while providing execution environments and common services for application programs. From a user perspective, an OS focuses on ease of use, performance, and resource availability. From a system perspective, the OS is a resource allocator and a control program. As a resource allocator, it decides between conflicting requests for CPU time, memory space, file-storage space, and I/O devices. As a control program, it manages the execution of user programs to prevent errors and improper use of the computer. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Bootstrap Program [Module 1 - Boot Architecture] Initial code stored in non-volatile ROM/EEPROM memory (firmware) that initializes hardware registers, memory controllers, and I/O devices, locates the operating system kernel on secondary storage, and loads it into RAM during boot up. Single-Processor Systems: Contains one main CPU capable of executing a general-purpose instruction set. Multiprocessor Systems (Parallel Systems / Tightly Coupled): Systems having two or more processors in close communication, sharing computer bus, clock, memory, and peripheral devices. Advantages include increased throughput, economy of scale, and increased reliability. Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP): Architecture where each processor runs an identical copy of the operating system and communicates as peers. All processors share physical memory. Asymmetric Multiprocessing: Architecture where each processor is assigned a specific task.

Advantages include increased throughput, economy of scale, and increased reliability. Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP): Architecture where each processor runs an identical copy of the operating system and communicates as peers. All processors share physical memory. Asymmetric Multiprocessing: Architecture where each processor is assigned a specific task. A master processor controls the system while slave processors wait for instructions or perform pre-assigned tasks. Clustered Systems: Combines two or more individual computer systems (nodes) coupled together via a storage-area network (SAN) or high-speed local area network (LAN) to provide high availability and fault tolerance. 1.2 Operating System Operations & Dual-Mode Execution Modern operating systems are interrupt-driven. Hardware interrupts signal event occurrences via system buses, while software interrupts (traps/exceptions) signal system errors or user software system call requests. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Dual-Mode Execution [Module 1 - Protection] Architectural protection mechanism that distinguishes between User Mode (mode bit = 1) and Kernel/Privileged Mode (mode bit = 0) to prevent rogue user processes from directly tampering with system hardware or memory. Mode switching occurs dynamically via hardware interrupts, traps, or system call invocations. When a user application invokes a system call, execution transitions from user mode to kernel mode by setting the mode bit to 0. Upon completing the system service, the kernel restores mode bit = 1 before returning control to the user application. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Timer Interrupt [Module 1 - CPU Control] A hardware device configured to trigger a periodic interrupt after a designated time quantum, ensuring the operating system kernel maintains control over the CPU and prevents user processes from monopolizing the system in infinite loops. 1.3 System Calls & System Services System calls provide a programmatic interface to services provided by the operating system.

1.3 System Calls & System Services System calls provide a programmatic interface to services provided by the operating system. Application programmers typically interact with high-level Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) such as Win32 API for Windows, POSIX API for UNIX/Linux, and Java API for Java Virtual Machines, rather than writing direct system call assembly routines. KEYWORD DEFINITION: System Call [Module 1 - System Interfaces] A specialized programming request invoked by a user application to request privileged kernel services from the operating system. Parameter passing during system call invocations is handled through three primary mechanisms: Register Passing: Parameters are stored directly in CPU registers. Fast, but limited by the total number of physical hardware registers. Block / Table Passing: Parameters are stored in a memory block/table, and the memory address of the block is passed as a single parameter in a CPU register. Stack Passing: Parameters are pushed onto the program stack by the application and popped off by the operating system kernel. Category Windows API Example UNIX System Call Example Process Control CreateProcess(), ExitProcess(), WaitForSingleObject() fork(), exit(), wait() File Management CreateFile(), ReadFile(), WriteFile(), CloseHandle() open(), read(), write(), close() Device Management SetConsoleMode(), ReadConsole(), WriteConsole() ioctl(), read(), write() Information Maintenance GetCurrentProcessID(), SetTimer(), Sleep() getpid(), alarm(), sleep() Communication CreatePipe(), CreateFileMapping(), MapViewOfFile() pipe(), shmget(), mmap() Protection SetFileSecurity(), InitializeSecurityDescriptor() chmod(), umask(), chown() 1.4 Operating System Structure & Design An operating system's internal organization balances performance, maintainability, modularity, and security across distinct architectural structures: Simple / Monolithic Structure: Lacks well-defined structure. Interfaces and levels of privilege are not well separated (e.g., original MS-DOS and early UNIX). High execution performance due to direct function calls, but highly susceptible to system-wide crashes from single component bugs. Layered Approach: The OS is broken into a number of discrete layers (levels). Layer 0 is hardware; Layer N is the user interface.

High execution performance due to direct function calls, but highly susceptible to system-wide crashes from single component bugs. Layered Approach: The OS is broken into a number of discrete layers (levels). Layer 0 is hardware; Layer N is the user interface. Each layer uses functions and services of lower layers only. Offers clean modularity and debugging, but suffers from performance overhead due to multi-layer call traversal. Microkernel Structure: Removes non-essential components from the kernel and implements them as user-level system applications (e.g., Mach kernel). Provides enhanced security and reliability, but experiences IPC performance bottlenecks. Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs): Modern object-oriented design approach where the kernel has a set of core components and dynamically loads additional services (such as file systems, device drivers, or network protocols) at boot or run time. 1.5 Process Management Concepts & PCB A process is an instance of a program in execution. While a program is a passive entity stored on disk (executable file), a process is an active entity with a program counter, CPU registers, and allocated system resources. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Process Memory Layout [Module 1 - Memory Layout] The dynamic structural division of a process's logical address space, comprising Text Section (executable machine code), Data Section (global and static variables), Heap Section (dynamically allocated memory), and Stack Section (local variables, function parameters, and return addresses). As a process executes, it transitions through distinct operational states: New: The process is currently being created. Running: Executable instructions are actively being processed by the CPU core. Waiting / Blocked: The process is suspended, awaiting an event occurrence such as I/O completion or signal reception. Ready: The process is loaded in main memory and waiting to be assigned to a CPU core. Terminated: The process has finished execution and its data structures are undergoing cleanup.

Ready: The process is loaded in main memory and waiting to be assigned to a CPU core. Terminated: The process has finished execution and its data structures are undergoing cleanup. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Process Control Block (PCB) [Module 1 - Process Management] A central kernel data structure (also termed task status block) containing all operational attributes of a process, including Process ID (PID), Program Counter, CPU registers, CPU scheduling info, memory-management info, accounting info, and I/O status info. 1.6 Process Scheduling & Queuing Management The process scheduler manages the assignment of available processes to CPU cores to meet objective criteria such as maximizing CPU utilization and maintaining interactive responsiveness. Job Queue: Holds all processes submitted to the system residing on secondary storage. Ready Queue: Holds all processes residing in main memory ready for execution. Device Queues: Holds processes waiting for access to specific I/O devices. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Schedulers [Module 1 - Process Scheduling] Specialized OS kernel components that manage process state transitions: Long-Term Scheduler (Job Scheduler) selects processes from disk job pool to memory controlling degree of multiprogramming; Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler) selects ready memory processes for CPU execution; Medium-Term Scheduler manages process swapping. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Context Switch [Module 1 - OS Dispatch] The state-saving and state-restoration procedure performed by the operating system when switching a CPU core from one process to another, saving current process state into its PCB and restoring the next process state from its PCB. 1.7 Operations on Processes & Inter-Process Communication Processes can create sub-processes dynamically forming a process tree. In UNIX/Linux systems, process creation is initiated via the fork() system call.

1.7 Operations on Processes & Inter-Process Communication Processes can create sub-processes dynamically forming a process tree. In UNIX/Linux systems, process creation is initiated via the fork() system call. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Zombie Process [Module 1 - Process Lifecycle] A terminated process whose parent has not yet invoked wait() to read its exit status, causing its entry to temporarily remain in the kernel process table. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Orphan Process [Module 1 - Process Lifecycle] An active process whose parent process terminated without calling wait(), resulting in the orphan process being inherited and adopted by the root init process (PID 1). Processes executing concurrently are either independent or cooperating. Cooperating processes require Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanisms: Shared Memory Model: Establishes a region of memory shared between processes. Communication speed is fast because access involves standard memory operations without kernel intervention after setup. Message Passing Model: Processes communicate by exchanging messages through kernel primitives (send/receive). Eliminates explicit memory locking, making it ideal for distributed environments. Module 2: Multithreaded Programming, CPU Scheduling & Process Synchronization 2.1 Multithreaded Programming & Thread Models A thread is a basic unit of CPU utilization, comprising a thread ID, a program counter, a register set, and a stack. Threads belonging to the same process share code section, data section, and operating system resources such as open files and signals. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Thread (Lightweight Process) [Module 2 - Multithreading] The smallest sequence of programmed instructions managed independently by an operating system scheduler, enabling concurrent execution paths within a single shared process memory space. Many-to-One Model: Maps many user-level threads to a single kernel thread. Efficient management in user space, but entire process blocks if a thread makes a blocking system call. One-to-One Model: Maps each user thread to a corresponding kernel thread.

Many-to-One Model: Maps many user-level threads to a single kernel thread. Efficient management in user space, but entire process blocks if a thread makes a blocking system call. One-to-One Model: Maps each user thread to a corresponding kernel thread. Provides true concurrency on multicore processors, but creating a user thread requires creating a corresponding kernel thread. Many-to-Many Model: Multiplexes many user-level threads to a smaller or equal number of kernel threads, balancing concurrency and thread creation overhead. 2.2 Thread Libraries & Threading Issues Thread libraries provide application programmers with APIs for creating and managing threads. Prominent thread libraries include POSIX Pthreads, Win32 Threads, and Java Threads. Fork / Exec Semantics: If a thread invokes fork(), some systems duplicate all threads while others duplicate only the calling thread. If exec() is called immediately after fork(), duplicating only the calling thread is sufficient. Signal Handling: Signals in UNIX notify processes of specific events. Signals can be handled by delivering to the thread to which the signal applies, delivering to every thread, or designating a specific thread to receive signals. Thread Cancellation: Terminating a thread before it finishes. Asynchronous cancellation terminates the target thread immediately, while Deferred cancellation allows the target thread to periodically check cancellation points. 2.3 CPU Scheduling Concepts & Criteria CPU scheduling forms the foundation of multiprogrammed operating systems. By switching the CPU among processes, the operating system makes the computer more productive. KEYWORD DEFINITION: CPU-I/O Burst Cycle [Module 2 - Scheduling] The operational lifecycle of process execution, consisting of alternating periods of CPU computation (CPU burst) and waiting for device inputs/outputs (I/O burst). CPU scheduling decisions occur under four circumstances: State Transition 1: When a process switches from running state to waiting state (e.g., I/O request).

CPU scheduling decisions occur under four circumstances: State Transition 1: When a process switches from running state to waiting state (e.g., I/O request). State Transition 2: When a process switches from running state to ready state (e.g., timer interrupt). State Transition 3: When a process switches from waiting state to ready state (e.g., I/O completion). State Transition 4: When a process terminates. Scheduling algorithms are evaluated using performance criteria: CPU Utilization: Percentage of time the CPU is actively executing instructions (target: 40% to 90%). Throughput: Number of completed processes per unit of time. Turnaround Time: Total interval from process submission to its complete execution. Waiting Time: Total time spent by a process sitting in the ready queue. Response Time: Time from process submission until the first response is produced. 2.4 CPU Scheduling Algorithms Algorithm Preemptive? Key Characteristic Major Drawback FCFS (First-Come First-Served) No Executes processes in order of arrival Convoy Effect (long wait for short jobs) SJF (Shortest Job Optional Schedules process with Requires future CPU First) (SRTF) shortest CPU burst prediction Priority Scheduling Optional Schedules process with highest priority number Indefinite starvation of low-priority jobs Round Robin (RR) Yes Allocates CPU for fixed time quantum (q) Performance heavily dependent on quantum size Multilevel Queue Varies Partitions ready queue into separate queues Fixed queue priorities cause starvation Multilevel Feedback Queue Yes Allows processes to move between queues High algorithmic complexity 2.5 Process Synchronization & Critical Section Problem Concurrent access to shared data may result in data inconsistency. Maintaining data consistency requires mechanisms to ensure the orderly execution of cooperating processes. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Race Condition [Module 2 - Synchronization] A flaw in concurrent systems where multiple processes access and manipulate the same shared data simultaneously, causing the final outcome to depend strictly on the unpredictable order of execution.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Race Condition [Module 2 - Synchronization] A flaw in concurrent systems where multiple processes access and manipulate the same shared data simultaneously, causing the final outcome to depend strictly on the unpredictable order of execution. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Critical Section [Module 2 - Synchronization] A segment of program code that accesses shared resources (such as shared variables, files, or tables) which must not be executed by more than one process at a time. A valid solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three essential criteria: 1. Mutual Exclusion: If process Pi is executing in its critical section, no other processes can execute in their critical sections. 2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and some processes wish to enter, only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which enters next. 3. Bounded Waiting: There must be a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted. 2.6 Software & Hardware Synchronization Solutions Peterson's Solution is a classic software-based solution for two processes. It assumes basic atomic LOAD and STORE instructions. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Peterson's Solution [Module 2 - Software Synchronization] A software synchronization algorithm for two processes (P0 and P1) using shared variables 'int turn' and 'boolean flag[2]', guaranteeing mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Hardware synchronization relies on atomic instructions that execute without interruption: TestAndSet(): Atomic hardware instruction that tests memory and returns its original value while simultaneously setting it to true. Swap(): Atomic hardware instruction that swaps the contents of two memory words. 2.7 Mutex Locks & Semaphores Operating systems provide higher-level software tools to solve the critical section problem without requiring raw assembly locking routines.

Swap(): Atomic hardware instruction that swaps the contents of two memory words. 2.7 Mutex Locks & Semaphores Operating systems provide higher-level software tools to solve the critical section problem without requiring raw assembly locking routines. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Semaphore [Module 2 - Synchronization Tools] A synchronization primitive consisting of an integer variable accessed exclusively through two atomic operations: wait() [P()] which decrements the count, and signal() [V()] which increments the count. Counting Semaphore: Integer value can range over an unrestricted domain, managing access to a finite set of resource instances. Binary Semaphore (Mutex Lock): Integer value ranges strictly between 0 and 1, providing simple mutual exclusion locks. Spinlock / Busy Waiting: A semaphore implementation where blocked processes loop continuously in entry code, wasting CPU cycles. Non-Busy Waiting Implementation: When a process executes wait() and finds the semaphore unavailable, it blocks itself and enters a wait queue associated with the semaphore. Executing signal() invokes wakeup() to move a blocked process to the ready queue. 2.8 Classical Synchronization Problems & Monitors Bounded-Buffer Problem: Producers add items to a finite buffer while consumers remove items. Synchronized using semaphores mutex (1), empty (N), and full (0). Readers-Writers Problem: Ensures multiple reader processes can read shared data simultaneously, but writer processes require exclusive access. Dining-Philosophers Problem: Models resource allocation challenges among processes competing for limited resources without causing deadlock or starvation. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Monitor [Module 2 - High-Level Synchronization] An abstract data type (ADT) construct that encapsulates shared data structures with a set of programmerdefined functions, enforcing mutual exclusion inside the monitor automatically. Module 3: Deadlocks & Main Memory Management 3.1 Deadlock Fundamentals & Characterization A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process holds a resource and waits for another resource held by another process in the set.

Module 3: Deadlocks & Main Memory Management 3.1 Deadlock Fundamentals & Characterization A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process holds a resource and waits for another resource held by another process in the set. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Deadlock [Module 3 - Deadlocks] A condition in concurrent systems where every process in a set is permanently waiting for an event or resource that can only be triggered or released by another waiting process in the set. A deadlock can arise if and only if four conditions hold simultaneously in a system: 1. Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode (only one process at a time can use the resource). 2. Hold and Wait: A process must be holding at least one resource and waiting to acquire additional resources currently held by other processes. 3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly preempted from a process; they can only be released voluntarily by the process after completing its task. 4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes exists ($P_0, P_1, \dots, P_n$) such that $P_0$ waits for a resource held by $P_1$, $P_1$ waits for $P_2$, and $P_n$ waits for $P_0$. 3.2 Deadlock Prevention & Avoidance Deadlock Prevention algorithms ensure that at least one of the four necessary conditions cannot hold. Preventing Hold & Wait: Require a process to request and be allocated all its required resources before execution begins, or allow requests only when holding zero resources. Preventing No Preemption: If a process holding resources requests another resource that cannot be immediately allocated, all currently held resources are preempted. Preventing Circular Wait: Impose a total global ordering of all resource types ($F: R o \mathbb{N}$) and require that processes request resources in strictly increasing order.

Preventing Circular Wait: Impose a total global ordering of all resource types ($F: R o \mathbb{N}$) and require that processes request resources in strictly increasing order. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Banker's Algorithm [Module 3 - Deadlock Avoidance] A deadlock avoidance algorithm for systems with multiple resource instances that determines whether granting a resource request leaves the system in a safe state, using data structures Available, Max, Allocation, and Need. 3.3 Deadlock Detection & Recovery If a system does not employ deadlock prevention or avoidance, it must provide detection and recovery algorithms: Process Termination: Abort all deadlocked processes, or abort deadlocked processes one at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated. Resource Preemption: Select a victim process, roll back its execution to a safe checkpoint state, and prevent process starvation by tracking rollback counts. 3.4 Main Memory Architecture & Address Space Main memory and registers are the only storage CPU cores can access directly. Programs must be loaded into memory to execute. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Address Binding [Module 3 - Memory Management] The mapping procedure that translates program variable references and code labels into absolute physical memory addresses, occurring at Compile Time, Load Time, or Execution Time. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Memory Management Unit (MMU) [Module 3 - Memory Hardware] A physical hardware device that performs real-time run-time mapping from logical (virtual) memory addresses to physical memory addresses using relocation registers. 3.5 Contiguous Memory Allocation & Fragmentation In contiguous memory allocation, each process is contained in a single contiguous section of memory. First-Fit: Allocates the first hole that is big enough. Fast search implementation. Best-Fit: Allocates the smallest hole that is big enough. Requires searching the entire list unless sorted by size; produces smallest leftover hole. Worst-Fit: Allocates the largest hole available. Produces largest leftover hole, but generally performs poorly in simulations.

Fast search implementation. Best-Fit: Allocates the smallest hole that is big enough. Requires searching the entire list unless sorted by size; produces smallest leftover hole. Worst-Fit: Allocates the largest hole available. Produces largest leftover hole, but generally performs poorly in simulations. KEYWORD DEFINITION: External Fragmentation [Module 3 - Memory Allocation] A memory condition where total available free memory space is sufficient to satisfy an allocation request, but the space is fragmented into many non-contiguous small blocks. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Internal Fragmentation [Module 3 - Memory Allocation] Unused memory space residing inside an allocated fixed-size frame or block due to the requested process memory being smaller than the allocated block size. 3.6 Paging & Segmentation Architecture Paging is a memory management scheme that permits a process's physical address space to be noncontiguous. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Paging [Module 3 - Paging] Memory allocation technique that divides physical memory into fixed-size blocks called Frames and divides program logical memory into blocks of the exact same size called Pages. Logical address generated by CPU is divided into Page Number (p) used as an index into a page table containing base physical frame address, and Page Offset (d) combined with base address to form physical memory location. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) [Module 3 - Memory Cache] A high-speed associative hardware cache used to store recent page-table translation entries, drastically reducing physical memory access time. Page table structures for large address spaces include Hierarchical (Two-Level) Paging, Hashed Page Tables, and Inverted Page Tables. Module 4: Virtual Memory Management & File System Implementation 4.1 Virtual Memory Fundamentals & Demand Paging Virtual memory separates user logical memory from physical memory. It allows execution of processes that are not completely loaded in physical memory.

Module 4: Virtual Memory Management & File System Implementation 4.1 Virtual Memory Fundamentals & Demand Paging Virtual memory separates user logical memory from physical memory. It allows execution of processes that are not completely loaded in physical memory. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Demand Paging [Module 4 - Virtual Memory] A virtual memory technique where pages are loaded into physical RAM only when they are explicitly referenced during execution (lazy swapper/pager). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Page Fault [Module 4 - Virtual Memory] A hardware interrupt raised by the Memory Management Unit when a process attempts to access a logical page that is currently marked invalid or not present in physical RAM. Handling a Page Fault involves six sequential steps: Step 1: The CPU references a page, prompting the MMU to check the page table valid-invalid bit. Step 2: If the bit is invalid, a page-fault trap is triggered to the operating system kernel. Step 3: The OS checks an internal table to verify whether the memory reference was a valid access or invalid access. Step 4: The OS locates a free frame on the physical memory free-frame list. Step 5: A disk read operation is scheduled to bring the requested page from secondary storage into the allocated frame. Step 6: The page table entry is updated (bit set to valid), internal state is updated, and the instruction that caused the trap is restarted. 4.2 Page Replacement Algorithms When physical memory is exhausted and a page fault occurs, page replacement algorithms select a victim frame to swap out to secondary storage.

4.2 Page Replacement Algorithms When physical memory is exhausted and a page fault occurs, page replacement algorithms select a victim frame to swap out to secondary storage. Page Replacement Algorithm Selection Strategy Key Property / Anomaly FIFO (First-In, First-Out) Replaces the oldest page brought into memory Suffers from Belady's Anomaly (page faults increase with more frames) Optimal (OPT / MIN) Replaces page that will not be used for longest future time Unrealizable in practice; serves as benchmark LRU (Least Recently Used) Replaces page that has not been used for longest past time High performance; requires hardware stack/counter support Second-Chance (Clock) FIFO variant using Reference Bit to give pages second chance Efficient circular queue implementation Enhanced Second-Chance Uses ordered pair (Reference Bit, Modify Bit) Prefers replacing clean nonmodified pages Counting-Based (LFU / MFU) Tracks page reference frequency counters Infrequently used due to high tracking overhead KEYWORD DEFINITION: Thrashing [Module 4 - Virtual Memory] A severe performance degradation condition where a system spends significantly more time swapping pages in and out of secondary storage than executing instructions, caused by inadequate physical frame allocation. 4.3 File System Interface & Structure The file system provides the mechanism for online storage and access to data and programs residing on secondary storage. KEYWORD DEFINITION: File [Module 4 - File Systems] A named logical collection of contiguous related information created by users and recorded on secondary storage devices. File Attributes: Name, Identifier, Type, Location, Size, Protection settings, and Timestamps. File Operations: Create, Write, Read, Reposition (lseek), Delete, and Truncate. Access Methods: Sequential Access (process reads all records in order), Direct/Random Access (process reads records in arbitrary order via block numbers), and Indexed Access.
