Access Methods: Sequential Access (process reads all records in order), Direct/Random Access (process reads records in arbitrary order via block numbers), and Indexed Access. 4.4 File System Implementation & Allocation Methods An operating system implements file systems using layered software abstractions, Virtual File System (VFS) interfaces, and File Control Blocks (FCB/Inodes). Contiguous Allocation: Requires each file to occupy a set of contiguous blocks on disk. Provides fast disk I/O performance, but suffers from external fragmentation and file growth limitations. Linked Allocation: Stores files as linked lists of disk blocks. Eliminates external fragmentation, but provides poor random access performance and introduces pointer storage overhead. Indexed Allocation: Brings all file block pointers together into an Index Block. Supports fast direct access without external fragmentation. KEYWORD DEFINITION: UNIX Inode Structure [Module 4 - File Systems] A multi-level indexed file allocation structure containing file metadata and direct block pointers, a single indirect pointer, a double indirect pointer, and a triple indirect pointer. Module 5: Mass Storage Structure, Protection & Linux Kernel Case Study 5.1 Mass Storage Structure & Disk Attachment Secondary mass storage systems, primarily magnetic hard disks and solid-state drives (SSDs), store the bulk of system and user data. Host-Attached Storage: Storage devices accessed directly through local hardware I/O buses (SATA, IDE, SAS). Network-Attached Storage (NAS): Storage appliance connected across a local area network (LAN) accessed via protocols such as NFS or CIFS. Storage Area Network (SAN): A high-speed dedicated storage network connecting servers and storage arrays using Fiber Channel or iSCSI interfaces. 5.2 Disk Scheduling Algorithms The operating system schedules I/O disk requests to minimize disk arm seek time and maximize total storage throughput.

Access Control Lists (ACLs): Each object maintains a list of domains and allowed operations (implementing columns of access matrix). Capability Lists: Each domain maintains a list of objects and allowed operations (implementing rows of access matrix). 5.4 Linux Kernel Architecture & Case Study Linux is a monolithic, highly modular, POSIX-compliant operating system kernel supporting symmetric multiprocessing, dynamic loadable kernel modules (LKMs), and preemptive execution. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Linux task_struct [Module 5 - Linux Kernel] The core process control block representation in the Linux kernel containing process state, execution scheduling priority, address space pointers (mm_struct), file descriptor tables (files_struct), and parent/child pointers.

Parallel Computing: Architectural Foundations, Programming Models, and Algorithmic Design A Comprehensive Theory & Reference Manual Based on Pacheco & Malensek (2nd Edition) Module 1: Parallel Hardware and Parallel Software Foundations 1.1 The Shift to Parallel Computing For decades, software performance improved continuously through microarchitectural innovations and increasing CPU clock frequencies. However, around 2005, single-core scaling encountered physical limitations commonly referred to as the 'Power Wall' and the 'Memory Wall'. Increasing clock speeds exponentially increased thermal dissipation ($P \propto V^2 f$), making air cooling unviable. Consequently, hardware manufacturers transitioned from building single, highly complex CPU cores to chip multiprocessors (CMP) and multi-core architectures. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Parallel Computing Definition: A computing paradigm in which multiple processing elements (threads, processor cores, or compute nodes) execute concurrently to solve a single computational problem. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: By decomposing a problem into smaller discrete sub-tasks that run simultaneously, parallel computing breaks through single-core throughput constraints, enabling highperformance processing across multi-core CPUs, clusters, and GPUs. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Power Wall Definition: The physical boundary where increasing CPU clock frequencies becomes impossible due to exponential thermal dissipation and power density limits. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Dynamic power consumption in CMOS circuits is governed by $P_{dynamic} = C \cdot V^2 \cdot f$. Beyond ~4 GHz, the power required and heat generated exceed the thermal dissipation capabilities of standard cooling solutions. 1.2 Flynn's Taxonomy of Computer Architectures In 1966, Michael J. Flynn proposed a classic classification scheme for computer architectures based on the number of concurrent instruction streams and data streams. SISD (Single Instruction, Single Data): Traditional von Neumann single-processor systems where one instruction stream acts on one data stream at a time.

Flynn proposed a classic classification scheme for computer architectures based on the number of concurrent instruction streams and data streams. SISD (Single Instruction, Single Data): Traditional von Neumann single-processor systems where one instruction stream acts on one data stream at a time. SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data): Vector processors and GPU execution units where a single control unit executes the same instruction simultaneously across multiple data items. MISD (Multiple Instruction, Single Data): A rare theoretical design where multiple instructions operate on the same data stream (e.g., fault-tolerant redundant systems). MIMD (Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data): Autonomous multi-core processors and distributed clusters where independent processors execute distinct instructions on distinct data streams. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Flynn's Taxonomy Definition: A classification of computer architectures into four distinct categories based on the multiplicity of hardware instruction streams and data streams. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Flynn's categorization provides the foundational vocabulary for distinguishing SIMD vector processing (found in multimedia extensions and GPUs) from MIMD multi-core and distributed processing systems. 1.3 Memory Architectures: Shared vs. Distributed Parallel hardware organization is fundamentally dictated by how physical memory is connected to the processing elements. Shared-Memory Systems (UMA vs. NUMA): All processors share a global address space. In Uniform Memory Access (UMA / Symmetric Multiprocessing), all memory locations exhibit identical access latencies. In Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA), memory is physically distributed among processor sockets; accessing local socket memory is significantly faster than accessing remote memory across interconnects. Distributed-Memory Systems: Each processing node possesses its own private physical memory and local address space. Nodes cannot directly read or write to another node's memory; communication occurs exclusively via message passing across a network interconnect. KEYWORD DEFINITION: NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) Definition: A shared-memory system architecture where memory access time depends on the physical location of the memory relative to the processor socket.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) Definition: A shared-memory system architecture where memory access time depends on the physical location of the memory relative to the processor socket. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: NUMA architectures scale shared memory to dozens or hundreds of cores by grouping processors and memory into nodes connected by high-speed interconnects (e.g., Intel UPI, AMD Infinity Fabric), requiring software optimization to maximize local memory allocations. 1.4 Cache Coherence and Memory Consistency In multi-core shared-memory systems, each core possesses private L1 and L2 caches. When multiple cores cache the same memory location, modifying data in one core's cache can lead to inconsistent memory views across the system. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Cache Coherence Definition: The hardware protocol ensuring that updates to any shared memory location are propagated throughout all cached copies across processing cores. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Snooping protocols monitor a shared bus to invalidate or update remote cache lines upon a write. Directory-based protocols maintain a central state table to track cache line locations in larger NUMA systems, avoiding broadcast traffic. KEYWORD DEFINITION: False Sharing Definition: A performance degradation phenomenon in shared-memory multi-core systems where independent variables used by different threads reside on the same cache line. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: When Thread A updates variable X and Thread B updates variable Y on the same 64-byte cache line, the underlying cache coherence hardware repeatedly invalidates the entire cache line across cores, causing severe memory bus thrashing ('cache ping-ponging'). 1.5 Interconnection Networks The network topology connecting processors and memory determines system bandwidth, latency, and scalability.

Partitioning: Decomposing the problem into small, discrete primitive tasks (Data Partitioning / Domain Decomposition or Task Partitioning / Functional Decomposition). 2. Communication: Determining the necessary data transfers, synchronization protocols, and dependencies between primitive tasks. 3. Agglomeration: Combining smaller primitive tasks into larger composite tasks to strike a balance between parallelism and communication overhead. 4. Mapping: Assigning composite agglomerated tasks to physical processing threads or nodes to ensure load balancing and minimize communication distance. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Foster's Design Methodology Definition: A structured four-phase algorithmic design strategy (Partitioning, Communication, Agglomeration, Mapping) for building efficient parallel software. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Foster's method guides developers from high-level problem specification down to hardware assignment, ensuring that task granularity matches target network latencies and processing power. Module 2: Distributed-Memory Programming with MPI 2.1 The Message-Passing Interface (MPI) Model The Message-Passing Interface (MPI) is a standardized, portable message-passing system specification designed for distributed-memory parallel architectures. In MPI, a set of autonomous processes (each with its own private address space) executes concurrently, communicating explicitly by sending and receiving messages across a network. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Message-Passing Interface (MPI) Definition: A standard library specification defining routines for explicit message passing and coordination among distributed processing nodes.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Message-Passing Interface (MPI) Definition: A standard library specification defining routines for explicit message passing and coordination among distributed processing nodes. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: MPI provides a SPMD (Single Program, Multiple Data) execution framework where processes run identical executable binaries, branching logically based on their assigned rank ID within a global communicator. KEYWORD DEFINITION: MPI Communicator Definition: An abstract object (`MPI_Comm`) defining a group of communicating processes that can safely exchange messages without interfering with other communication contexts. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: `MPI_COMM_WORLD` is the default communicator created at initialization, encapsulating all processes launched by `mpirun` or `mpiexec`. 2.2 Core Environment and Process Management Every MPI program begins by establishing the execution context with `MPI_Init` and concludes by releasing resources via `MPI_Finalize`. // C MPI Environment Setup and Process Identification #include <stdio.h> #include <mpi.h> int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { int my_rank, comm_sz; MPI_Init(&argc, &argv); MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &my_rank); MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &comm_sz); printf("Hello from rank %d of %d processes\n", my_rank, comm_sz); MPI_Finalize(); return 0; 2.3 Point-to-Point Communication Mechanics Point-to-point communication involves explicit message transfers between a single sender process and a single receiver process. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Point-to-Point Communication Definition: Direct transmission of data from one specific process (source rank) to another specific process (destination rank) using `MPI_Send` and `MPI_Recv`. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Messages are uniquely matched based on four criteria: Source Rank, Destination Rank, Message Tag (an integer identifier), and Communicator context. MPI_Send Signature: `int MPI_Send(void* buf, int count, MPI_Datatype datatype, int dest, int tag, MPI_Comm comm)` MPI_Recv Signature: `int MPI_Recv(void* buf, int count, MPI_Datatype datatype, int source, int tag, MPI_Comm comm, MPI_Status* status)` KEYWORD DEFINITION: Non-Blocking Communication Definition: Communication routines (`MPI_Isend`, `MPI_Irecv`) that post a transmission request and return control immediately to the calling thread without waiting for completion.

Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Non-blocking primitives allow applications to overlap communication with computation. Completion must be explicitly verified using `MPI_Wait` or `MPI_Test` before accessing buffers. 2.4 Collective Communication Primitives Collective communication involves all processes within a communicator simultaneously participating in a coordinated operation. MPI_Init(&argc, &argv); MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &my_rank); MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &comm_sz); h = (b - a) / n; local_n = n / comm_sz; local_a = a + my_rank * local_n * h; local_b = local_a + local_n * h; local_int = Trap(local_a, local_b, local_n, h); MPI_Reduce(&local_int, &total_int, 1, MPI_DOUBLE, MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD); if (my_rank == 0) { printf("Integral Result = %e\n", total_int); MPI_Finalize(); return 0; 2.5 Derived Datatypes and Custom Data Structures MPI derived datatypes allow processes to transmit non-contiguous memory blocks or heterogeneous structures in a single message, avoiding manual buffer packing overhead. KEYWORD DEFINITION: MPI Derived Datatype Definition: A user-defined datatype construction that describes non-contiguous or mixed-type memory layouts for unified MPI transmission. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Built using `MPI_Type_contiguous`, `MPI_Type_vector`, or `MPI_Type_create_struct`, derived datatypes must be registered via `MPI_Type_commit` prior to transmission. Module 3: Shared-Memory Programming with Pthreads 3.1 POSIX Threads Execution Model POSIX Threads (Pthreads) is a standardized C/C++ thread management API defining low-level primitives for thread creation, join operations, and mutual exclusion in shared-memory multi-core environments. KEYWORD DEFINITION: POSIX Thread (Pthread) Definition: An independent kernel-level or user-level execution thread operating within the shared address space of a single process. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Pthreads share global variables, heap memory, file descriptors, and environment settings, but retain independent call stacks, registers, and thread IDs.

Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Pthreads share global variables, heap memory, file descriptors, and environment settings, but retain independent call stacks, registers, and thread IDs. 3.2 Thread Lifecycle and API Creation Threads are spawned using `pthread_create` and joined back into the main execution thread via `pthread_join`. // Pthreads Lifecycle and Parallel Work Assignment #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #include <pthread.h> #define NUM_THREADS 4 void* ThreadWork(void* rank) { long my_rank = (long) rank; printf("Pthread worker running on thread ID %ld\n", my_rank); return NULL; int main() { pthread_t thread_handles[NUM_THREADS]; for (long thread = 0; thread < NUM_THREADS; thread++) { pthread_create(&thread_handles[thread], NULL, ThreadWork, (void*) thread); for (long thread = 0; thread < NUM_THREADS; thread++) { pthread_join(thread_handles[thread], NULL); return 0; 3.3 Race Conditions and Critical Sections Because threads access a shared heap and static global memory, non-atomic concurrent updates to shared variables produce race conditions. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Critical Section Definition: A code segment accessing shared resources that must not be concurrently executed by more than one thread. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Failure to enforce mutual exclusion across critical sections causes nondeterministic data corruption and race conditions. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Mutex (Mutual Exclusion Lock) Definition: A synchronization lock (`pthread_mutex_t`) designed to enforce single-thread access to a critical section. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: A thread calls `pthread_mutex_lock` to acquire ownership. If locked, the caller blocks until `pthread_mutex_unlock` releases the lock. 3.4 Advanced Synchronization: Condition Variables and Barriers Complex coordination requires notification primitives rather than simple mutual exclusion. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Condition Variable Definition: A synchronization object (`pthread_cond_t`) enabling threads to suspend execution until a specific predicate condition is signaled by another thread. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: `pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex)` atomically releases the associated mutex and blocks the thread, re-acquiring the mutex upon being woken by `pthread_cond_signal` or `pthread_cond_broadcast`.

Theoretical Context & Mechanics: `pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex)` atomically releases the associated mutex and blocks the thread, re-acquiring the mutex upon being woken by `pthread_cond_signal` or `pthread_cond_broadcast`. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Barrier Synchronization Definition: A point in parallel code execution where all participating threads must arrive before any thread is permitted to proceed. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: `pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier)` ensures that multi-phase parallel algorithms complete Phase N across all threads before starting Phase N+1. Module 4: Shared-Memory Programming with OpenMP 4.1 OpenMP Architecture and Fork-Join Pattern OpenMP (Open Multi-Processing) is a directive-based API that simplifies shared-memory parallel programming in C, C++, and Fortran using compiler pragma directives, runtime library functions, and environment variables. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Fork-Join Execution Model Definition: The core parallel execution model where a single master thread executes sequentially until encountering a parallel region, at which point it forks a team of worker threads to execute parallel tasks, joining back into a single master thread upon completion. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: The fork-join structure allows incremental parallelization of sequential legacy applications without rewriting complete core logic. 4.2 Parallel Directives and Scope Clauses The fundamental building block is `#pragma omp parallel`, which creates a team of threads to execute the enclosed structured block. private(var): Creates a thread-private instance of `var` for each thread (uninitialized). firstprivate(var): Creates a thread-private instance initialized with the value prior to the parallel region. shared(var): All threads access the same original memory location for `var`. reduction(op:var): Creates thread-private copies accumulated locally and combined into the global original variable at region exit using operator `op` (+, *, max, min). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Reduction Clause Definition: An OpenMP clause that performs associative combining operations across thread-local variables without explicit locking overhead. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: `reduction(+:total)` prevents race conditions during accumulation while eliminating mutex contention across iterations.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Reduction Clause Definition: An OpenMP clause that performs associative combining operations across thread-local variables without explicit locking overhead. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: `reduction(+:total)` prevents race conditions during accumulation while eliminating mutex contention across iterations. 4.3 Work-Sharing Constructs and Scheduling Strategies Work-sharing constructs divide loop iterations among the executing thread team. // OpenMP Parallel Loop with Reduction Clause #include <stdio.h> #include <omp.h> int main() { double sum = 0.0; int n = 1000000; #pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum) schedule(static) for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += (i * 0.5); printf("Computed Sum = %f\n", sum); return 0; Schedule Type Chunk Allocation Strategy Overhead Level Best Use Case static Round-robin allocation of fixed-size chunks at compile time Lowest Uniform loop iteration workloads dynamic Runtime allocation from dynamic Medium-High Highly imbalanced task queue as threads finish iteration execution times guided Dynamically decreasing chunk sizes proportional to remaining work Medium Imbalanced workloads with heavy early iterations auto Delegates schedule selection to compiler/runtime optimizer Variable Generalized automated tuning runtime Defines schedule at runtime via `OMP_SCHEDULE` environment variable Configurable Experimental performance profiling 4.4 Task-Based Parallelism For irregular problems (tree traversal, pointer chasing, recursion), OpenMP 3.0 introduced tasking primitives (`#pragma omp task`). KEYWORD DEFINITION: OpenMP Task Definition: An independent unit of work packaged with its execution code and data context, queued for execution by any available thread in the current team. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Tasking decouples work generation from execution, enabling effective load balancing in highly irregular and unstructured applications. Module 5: Massively Parallel Heterogeneous Computing with CUDA 5.1 The GPGPU Heterogeneous Computing Model Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) are specialized hardware accelerators engineered for massive data parallelism. CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is NVIDIA's parallel computing platform allowing developers to write C/C++ code executing on GPU hardware.

CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is NVIDIA's parallel computing platform allowing developers to write C/C++ code executing on GPU hardware. KEYWORD DEFINITION: CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) Definition: A software API and computing platform enabling general-purpose compute (GPGPU) execution on NVIDIA GPU graphics hardware. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: CUDA splits application execution between the Host CPU (sequential control code) and the Device GPU (massively parallel compute kernels). 5.2 CUDA Thread Hierarchy CUDA structures massive thread execution into a 3-tier hierarchy: Threads, Thread Blocks, and Grids. Thread: The basic unit of execution executing a CUDA kernel function. Thread Block: A software grouping of up to 1024 threads scheduled on a single Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), sharing Shared Memory and hardware barrier synchronization. Grid: A collection of thread blocks launched simultaneously to execute a GPU kernel. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Warp Definition: A group of 32 contiguous CUDA threads within a thread block that execute instructions simultaneously in SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) lockstep. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: If threads within a warp diverge along different conditional execution branches (`if/else`), the SM serializes branch paths ('Warp Divergence'), severely degrading performance. 5.3 Spatial Thread Indexing Formulas CUDA provides built-in variables (`threadIdx`, `blockIdx`, `blockDim`, `gridDim`) to determine a thread's unique global index within a 1D, 2D, or 3D domain. 1D Global Thread Index Formula: `int global_id = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;` 2D Global Thread Index Formula (e.g., Matrix): `int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y; int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;` 5.4 CUDA Memory Hierarchy Effective GPU programming relies on managing distinct hardware memory spaces.

Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Coalesced accesses combine 32 thread memory requests into a single hardware transaction, maximizing GPU memory bandwidth utilization. Module 6: Parallel Algorithms, Performance Metrics, and Scalability 6.1 Performance Evaluation Metrics Measuring parallel application efficiency requires defining exact speedup and utilization metrics.

Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Coalesced accesses combine 32 thread memory requests into a single hardware transaction, maximizing GPU memory bandwidth utilization. Module 6: Parallel Algorithms, Performance Metrics, and Scalability 6.1 Performance Evaluation Metrics Measuring parallel application efficiency requires defining exact speedup and utilization metrics. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Speedup (S_p) Definition: The ratio of sequential execution time on a single core ($T_{serial}$) to parallel execution time on $p$ cores ($T_{parallel}$). Theoretical Context & Mechanics: $S_p = \frac{T_{serial}}{T_{parallel}}$. Linear speedup ($S_p = p$) represents ideal, perfect scaling. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Efficiency (E_p) Definition: The average fraction of time each processor core is actively performing useful compute work. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: $E_p = \frac{S_p}{p} = \frac{T_{serial}}{p \cdot T_{parallel}}$. Perfectly parallelized programs yield $E_p = 1.0$ (100%). 6.2 Amdahl's Law vs. Gustafson-Barsis Law Two complementary theoretical models evaluate parallel speedup limits based on problem scaling assumptions. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Amdahl's Law Definition: A model governing fixed-size problem scaling that proves parallel speedup is fundamentally bottlenecked by the strictly sequential fraction of a workload. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: $S_p = \frac{1}{\gamma + \frac{1 - \gamma}{p}}$, where $\gamma$ is the sequential fraction. If $\gamma = 10\%$, maximum theoretical speedup can never exceed 10x, regardless of processor count. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Gustafson-Barsis Law Definition: A model governing weak scaling where problem size expands proportionally with available processor core count. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: $S_p = p - \gamma (p - 1)$. Proves that massive speedup is attainable on ultra-large datasets by scaling data volume as hardware expands. 6.3 Parallel Sorting Networks: Bitonic Sort Bitonic sort is a classic parallel sorting algorithm engineered for SIMD hypercubes and GPU thread blocks. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Bitonic Sequence Definition: A sequence of numbers $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}$ that monotonically increases and then monotonically decreases, or can be circularly shifted to satisfy this condition.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Bitonic Sequence Definition: A sequence of numbers $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}$ that monotonically increases and then monotonically decreases, or can be circularly shifted to satisfy this condition. Theoretical Context & Mechanics: Bitonic sort constructs and merges bitonic sequences recursively in $O(\log^2 n)$ parallel steps using deterministic Compare-and-Swap operations. PART I: VACCINATION TRUST, RISK COMMUNICATION & CRISIS MITIGATION Chapter 1: Public Health Foundations of Vaccination & Institutional Trust Vaccines represent one of the most cost-effective and powerful public health interventions in medical history, directly reducing child mortality and controlling infectious disease transmission worldwide. Beyond immediate biomedical protection, vaccination programs yield profound socioeconomic returns, fostering poverty reduction, educational attainment, health equity, and overall health system resilience. However, because vaccines are administered to healthy individuals—predominantly infants and children—public scrutiny regarding vaccine safety, quality, and necessity is exceptionally high. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Vaccine A biological product designed to stimulate an individual's immune system to produce adaptive immunity against a specific pathogen, thereby preventing or attenuating disease. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Vaccination The clinical action of administering a vaccine to an individual (via injection, oral drops, or nasal spray) to induce active immunity. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Immunization The biological process whereby a person becomes protected against a disease through vaccination or natural infection. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Vaccination Services The organizational, financial, and clinical infrastructure through which vaccines are delivered in a country, including physical access, cost structures, clinic operating hours, and healthcare provider competency. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Vaccination Schedule An officially recommended or mandated timetable detailing the specific age, dosage, and interval timing for administering required vaccines to a population. When unwanted medical events occur following vaccination—whether causally linked to the vaccine or purely coincidental—they have the potential to trigger public anxiety, erode institutional trust, and severely impair immunization coverage.

When unwanted medical events occur following vaccination—whether causally linked to the vaccine or purely coincidental—they have the potential to trigger public anxiety, erode institutional trust, and severely impair immunization coverage. Public health authorities must maintain proactive communication strategies and robust preparedness frameworks to navigate potential safety scares before they escalate into societal crises. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Population Resilience The collective capacity of a population to understand the risks and benefits of immunization, critically evaluate health information, and maintain confidence in health authorities after experiencing adverse events or antivaccination rumors. Chapter 2: Psychological Determinants of Vaccine Decision-Making Vaccine decision-making is a multi-dimensional psychological process governed by cognitive risk evaluations, emotional processing, social influences, and environmental conditions. Public health communication must be grounded in established behavioral science models, including the Health Belief Model, the Theory of Planned Behavior, and the Health Action Process Approach. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Risk Perception An individual's subjective assessment of the likelihood (probability) and severity (consequences) of a negative future event, heavily influenced by emotional reactions and cognitive heuristics rather than statistical data alone. Cognitive Heuristics in Vaccine Risk Processing Because human beings are not perfect information processors, individuals rely on cognitive shortcuts (heuristics) when processing complex health information under uncertainty. While these shortcuts reduce mental effort, they frequently lead to systematic biases: Affect Heuristic: Guiding judgments based on immediate emotional reactions (e.g., fear, anxiety, or outrage) rather than objective statistical evidence. Safety Effect (Loss Aversion): The psychological tendency to focus disproportionately on avoiding potential losses or harms (e.g., vaccine side effects) over securing future gains (e.g., disease immunity). Confirmation Bias: The tendency to selectively seek, interpret, and recall information that confirms pre-existing beliefs regarding vaccine safety or institutional trust.

Confirmation Bias: The tendency to selectively seek, interpret, and recall information that confirms pre-existing beliefs regarding vaccine safety or institutional trust. Availability Heuristic: Evaluating risk based on how easily specific instances come to mind, making recent, vivid, or emotionally charged media reports heavily influential. Adjustment and Anchoring Heuristic: Basing decisions on an initial familiar position or opinion (the anchor) and making insufficient adjustments when exposed to new counter-evidence. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Social Norms Shared behavioral rules and expectations within a group that dictate how members ought to behave (injunctive norms) or describe how most members actually behave (descriptive norms). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Habit Automatic behavioral patterns established through past repetition; past vaccination compliance is one of the strongest empirical predictors of future vaccine acceptance. Chapter 3: Vaccine Hesitancy, Safety Scares & Historical Case Studies Vaccine hesitancy exists along a continuum ranging from passive delay to active refusal. Understanding the root causes of hesitancy is vital for designing targeted interventions and preventing localized concerns from expanding into global safety scares. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Vaccine Hesitancy A delay in the acceptance or outright refusal of vaccines despite the availability of vaccination services. It is complex, context-specific, and varies across time, place, and specific vaccines. The 3 Cs Model of Vaccine Hesitancy The WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) Working Group categorizes the primary determinants of vaccine hesitancy into three core pillars: Pillar Core Psychological Mechanism Impact on Vaccination Behavior Complacency Low perceived risk of vaccine-preventable diseases; disease seen as distant, rare, or mild. Vaccination is not viewed as a necessary health priority, leading to low demand. Convenience Structural barriers including physical distance, financial cost, clinic hours, and low health literacy. Even when positive intent exists, physical or operational friction prevents action. Confidence Distrust in vaccine efficacy, safety, healthcare providers, or policymaker motives.

Convenience Structural barriers including physical distance, financial cost, clinic hours, and low health literacy. Even when positive intent exists, physical or operational friction prevents action. Confidence Distrust in vaccine efficacy, safety, healthcare providers, or policymaker motives. Fear of adverse reactions and institutional suspicion leads to active refusal. Historical Case Studies & Crisis Dynamics Historical analysis reveals that anti-vaccination movements and safety scares follow predictable patterns of escalation: 19th Century Compulsory Smallpox Acts (UK): Following mandatory smallpox vaccination laws passed between 1840 and 1853, anti-vaccination leagues organized massive protests, culminating in the 1885 Leicester demonstration involving up to 100,000 marchers challenging state infringement on civil liberties. Pertussis Vaccine Controversy (1970s–1980s): Widespread media coverage of alleged neurological reactions following whole-cell pertussis vaccination led to public panic, suspension of pertussis immunization in several nations, and a subsequent 10- to 100-fold increase in pertussis incidence. German HPV Vaccine Crisis (2007): Following HPV vaccine recommendations, 13 scientists published a online statement claiming unverified efficacy and industry bias. Despite scientific refutation by STIKO, intense emotional media framing reduced HPV coverage to 25% among target adolescent populations. Israeli Influenza Vaccine Incident: Four elderly men with chronic heart conditions died shortly after receiving influenza vaccine from the same batch. Media coverage led to a temporary campaign suspension. Although a 4-day investigation confirmed natural cardiac causes, public panic caused a sharp drop in vaccine uptake, leading to an increase in winter pneumonia mortality among the elderly. Andrew Wakefield MMR Study (1998): A fraudulent 12-patient study alleged a causal link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Despite full retraction, ethical sanctions, and extensive scientific refutation, media amplification caused decades of lingering misperceptions and recurrent measles outbreaks across Europe.

Andrew Wakefield MMR Study (1998): A fraudulent 12-patient study alleged a causal link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Despite full retraction, ethical sanctions, and extensive scientific refutation, media amplification caused decades of lingering misperceptions and recurrent measles outbreaks across Europe. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Dual Relationship Model The bi-directional feedback mechanism wherein baseline vaccine hesitancy renders a population highly vulnerable to safety rumors, while unmitigated safety scares rapidly amplify baseline hesitancy. Chapter 4: Risk Communication, Message Design & Audience Engagement When responding to events that threaten public confidence, public health institutions must deploy structured risk communication frameworks to manage uncertainty, correct misperceptions, and build enduring institutional trust. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Crisis An unexpected, non-routine event or series of events that creates high levels of uncertainty, surprise, and perceived threat to public health or organizational reputation. The Four Pillars of Institutional Trust Institutional trust is built and preserved across four core operational dimensions: 1. Competence: Demonstrating technical mastery, scientific accuracy, and reliable healthcare delivery. 2. Consistency: Ensuring predictable, aligned messaging and transparent actions across all public health agencies. 3. Sincerity: Maintaining complete honesty, openness regarding uncertainties, and radical transparency. 4. Faith (Empathy): Proactively listening to public concerns, validating emotions, and demonstrating genuine care for community well-being. Message Framing and Misinformation Debunking Rules When designing public communications, framing and structure dictate how messages are received: Gain Frames vs. Loss Frames: Gain frames (focusing on positive health protection and rights) are significantly more effective for preventive behaviors like vaccination than loss frames (focusing on disease suffering). Fear Appeals: Eliciting fear should generally be avoided unless addressing severe complacency. To be effective, fear appeals must recommend a clear, one-time action and provide high self-efficacy guidance.

To be effective, fear appeals must recommend a clear, one-time action and provide high self-efficacy guidance. Rules for Debunking Misinformation: 1) Lead with the core fact, not the myth; 2) Keep explanations simple and memorable; 3) Provide explicit warnings before referencing a myth; 4) Offer a clear alternative explanation replacing the false narrative; 5) Avoid repeating the myth to prevent accidental reinforcement. PART II: WHO INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES (ICD-11) REFERENCE GUIDE Chapter 5: Overview, Purpose & Governance of ICD-11 The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is the global ontological standard for recording, reporting, and grouping health conditions, diseases, external causes of injury, and clinical manifestations. Maintained by the World Health Organization (WHO) pursuant to legal mandates under the WHO Nomenclature Regulations, ICD-11 represents the eleventh revision, incorporating digitalnative architecture, semantic interoperability, and modern medical science. KEYWORD DEFINITION: International Classification of Diseases (ICD) The standard diagnostic tool for epidemiology, health management, and clinical purposes, allowing systematic recording, analysis, interpretation, and comparison of mortality and morbidity data worldwide. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Semantic Interoperability The technical capability of digital health systems to exchange clinical data with unambiguous, shared meaning across disparate software, institutions, and international borders.

KEYWORD DEFINITION: Semantic Interoperability The technical capability of digital health systems to exchange clinical data with unambiguous, shared meaning across disparate software, institutions, and international borders. The WHO Family of International Classifications (WHO-FIC) The WHO-FIC framework establishes standardized, integrated building blocks for global health statistics across three structural tiers: Reference Classifications: Cover core parameters of health systems: ICD (Death & Disease), ICF (International Classification of Functioning, Disability & Health), and ICHI (International Classification of Health Interventions). Derived Classifications: Specialty linearizations derived from core classifications, such as ICD-O (Oncology) and primary care adaptations. Related Classifications: Complementary tools covering specialized health domains, including ICPC (Primary Care), ICECI (External Causes of Injury), ATC/DDD (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical Classification), and ICNP (Nursing Practice). Chapter 6: Structural Taxonomy & Conventions of ICD-11 departs fundamentally from paper-bound historical revisions by establishing a digital-native, two-tier architecture comprising an underlying multidimensional database and specialized linearizations. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Foundation Component The underlying multi-dimensional database holding all ICD entities, concepts, terms, URIs, and relationships from which tabular lists and specialized linearizations are derived. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Linearization A subset of the Foundation Component structured into a mutually exclusive, mono-hierarchical tabular list tailored for specific operational uses (e.g., Mortality and Morbidity Statistics - MMS). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Stem Code The primary alphanumeric code assigned to a distinct diagnostic entity in a tabular list (e.g., 1B10 for Respiratory Tuberculosis). KEYWORD DEFINITION: Extension Code Supplementary codes (starting with 'X') used exclusively via postcoordination to qualify stem codes with detailed information regarding anatomy, etiology, severity, or temporal parameters. KEYWORD DEFINITION: Postcoordination The clinical coding process of linking two or more codes together (using ampersands '&' or slashes '/') to capture a complex, fully detailed clinical concept.

Overview and Epistemological Framework of IKS Indian Knowledge System (IKS) encompasses the comprehensive repository of knowledge generated, codified, and sustained by the Indian civilization over at least five millennia. Unlike modern western paradigms that frequently segregate sacred and secular inquiries, IKS provides a unified framework connecting spiritual realization, intellectual rigor, material prosperity (abhyudaya), and ultimate liberation (niśśreyasa). A defining structural feature of IKS is its dual transmission methodology: the rigorous oral tradition (Śruti) preserved through sophisticated mnemonic devices and phonetic rules, alongside codified literary texts (Smṛti and Śāstras). The repository encompasses both religious philosophy (Sanātana-dharma, Buddhist, and Jaina traditions) and extensive practical disciplines including metallurgy, linguistics, astronomy, medicine, statecraft, and architecture. 2. The Vedic Corpus and Caturdaśa-Vidyāsthāna The foundation of traditional Indian learning is organized under the Caturdaśa-Vidyāsthāna—the fourteen primary abodes of knowledge. These comprise the Four Vedas, the Six Vedāṅgas, the Purāṇas, Mīmāṁsā, Nyāya, and Dharma-śāstra. Each Veda is structurally subdivided into four textual layers: • Saṁhitā: Core collection of mantras and poetic hymns. • Brāhmaṇa: Prose texts elucidating ritual significance and esoteric meanings. • Āraṇyaka: Forest treatises focusing on symbolic and meditative interpretations. • Upaniṣad: Philosophical dialogues addressing the ultimate nature of reality (Brahman), the self (Ātman), and liberation. 3. Philosophical Systems (Darśanas) Indian philosophy is systematically categorized into Āstika (Vedic/Orthodox) schools, which accept the authority of the Vedas, and Nāstika (Heterodox) schools, which reject Vedic authority. The Six Vedic Schools (Ṣaḍ-Darśana) 1. Sāṁkhya (Kapila): Dualistic cosmology postulating Puruṣa (pure consciousness) and Prakṛti (primordial matter transformed through the three Guṇas). 2. Yoga (Patañjali): Practical eight-folded path (Aṣṭāṅga-yoga) for mental mastery, meditation, and spiritual liberation. 3. Nyāya (Gautama): Epistemological school emphasizing rigorous logic, debate methodology, and four valid means of knowledge (Pramāṇas). 4. Vaiśeṣika (Kaṇāda): Atomistic physical cosmology classifying reality into six categories (Padārthas) including Dravya (substance) and Paramāṇu (indivisible atoms). 5. Pūrva-Mīmāṁsā (Jaimini): Hermeneutical science of textual interpretation and ritual duty (Dharma). 6. Uttara-Mīmāṁsā / Vedānta (Bādarāyaṇa): Non-dualistic (Advaita), qualified non-dualistic (Viśiṣṭādvaita), and dualistic (Dvaita) inquiries into spiritual reality. Non-Vedic Traditions • Bauddha Darśana: Focuses on the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, Pratītyasamutpāda (dependent origination), and Nirvana. • Jaina Darśana: Emphasizes Ahiṁsā (non-violence), Anekāntavāda (manifold aspects of truth), Syādvāda (conditional predication), and strict ascetic ethics. • Cārvāka / Lokāyata: Materialist school accepting only direct sensory perception (Pratyakṣa) as valid knowledge. Part 2: Foundational Concepts for Science & Technology 1. Linguistics, Phonetics, and Sanskrit Grammar Architecture Linguistics holds a central position in IKS. Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī (c. 6th century BCE) represents the world's earliest formal generative grammar. Containing approximately 3,983 concise rules (sūtras), the system operates much like a modern programming language compiler, generating valid word forms from basic roots (dhātus) and suffixes (pratyayas). The phonetic backbone of Sanskrit grammar is codified in the 14 Māheśvara-sūtras, which group speech sounds based on their articulation points (throat, palate, teeth, lips) and phonetic features. This rulebased, algorithmic architecture makes Sanskrit exceptionally suitable for natural language processing (NLP), knowledge representation, and computational linguistics. 2. Numeral Systems, Place Value, and Binary Mathematics Ancient India pioneered the decimal place-value system and the mathematical concept of Zero (Śūnya) as both a placeholder and an operational number. This innovation revolutionized global calculation capabilities. To record large numbers seamlessly within poetic and oral texts, Indian scholars created sophisticated verbal numeral systems: • Bhūta-saṁkhyā System: Words representing known quantities (e.g., 'Netra' or 'Aksi' for 2, 'Veda' for 4, 'Rasa' for 6) are combined to form multi-digit numbers. • Kaṭapayādi System: Assigns numerical values (0–9) to specific Sanskrit consonants, allowing scholars to embed astronomical constants and mathematical tables into meaningful verses. In Chandah-śāstra (c. 300 BCE), Piṅgala developed a formal system of prosody that established the foundations of binary mathematics. By classifying poetic meters as Laghu (light / 1) and Guru (heavy / 0), Piṅgala described binary combinations, combinatorial arrangements (Prastāra), conversion algorithms between binary and decimal numbers (Naṣṭa and Uddiṣṭa), and the binomial coefficient triangle (Meruprastāra, later known in the West as Pascal's Triangle). 3.

Measurement Systems for Time, Length, and Weight Ancient Indian literature documents a vast, unified system of standardized units ranging from microscopic atomic dimensions to cosmic time scales. Mathematics and Geometry Indian mathematical development was driven by both practical ritual requirements and scientific inquiry. The Śulba-sūtras (Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana, c. 800–500 BCE) detail sophisticated geometrical principles used in constructing Vedic altars (yajña-vedis). They explicitly record the Pythagorean theorem prior to Pythagoras, methods for squaring the circle, and accurate approximations for the square root of 2 (√2 ≈ 1.4142156). Classical mathematicians expanded these foundations: • Āryabhaṭa I (476 CE): In Āryabhaṭīya, defined sine (jya) and versine (utkrama-jya), calculated π to 3.1416, and provided exact algorithms for integer solutions, square roots, and cube roots. • Brahmagupta (598 CE): In Brāhma-sphuṭa-siddhānta, formulated complete mathematical rules for operations involving Zero and negative numbers, quadratic equations, and cyclic quadrilaterals. • Bhāskara II (1114 CE): Author of Līlāvatī and Bījagaṇita, introduced calculus concepts, zero division properties, and general solutions to indeterminate equations (Pell's equation / Cakravalā method). • Kerala School of Mathematics (Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma, 14th century): Pioneered infinite series for π, sine, and cosine functions, anticipating European calculus by over two centuries. 2.

Astronomy and Astronomical Instruments Indian mathematical astronomy (Jyotiṣa-śāstra) developed advanced models for tracking planetary motion, predicting eclipses, and calculating planetary positions on a spherical Earth. Key developments include the geocentric models of Āryabhaṭa and Nilakaṇṭha Somayājī, the accurate division of the ecliptic into 27 Nakṣatras and 12 Rāśis, and the formulation of the Indian calendar system (Pañcāṅga) tracking Tithi, Vāra, Nakṣatra, Yoga, and Karaṇa. To validate calculations against observational reality, scholars constructed sophisticated physical instruments (Yantras), including the Gola-yantra (armillary sphere), Nāḍīvalaya-yantra (equatorial sundial), Cakra-yantra, and the monumental masonry observatories (Jantar Mantar) constructed by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in Jaipur, Delhi, Ujjain, and Varanasi. 3. Metallurgy and Materials Science Ancient India was an acknowledged global leader in extractive metallurgy and materials processing. Excavations at Zawar (Rajasthan) reveal the world's earliest industrial-scale zinc production using a specialized downward drift distillation technique dating back to 400 BCE. Notable metallurgical achievements include: • Wootz Steel: High-carbon crucible steel produced in South India, exported globally for manufacturing legendary Damascus blades. • Corrosion-Resistant Iron: Exemplified by the 1,600-year-old Iron Pillar of Delhi (6 tonnes) and the Konark iron beams, manufactured through forge-welding wrought iron with high phosphorus content that formed a protective passive layer. • Lost-Wax Bronze Casting (Madhūcchiṣṭa-vidhānam): Mastered during the Harappan period and perfected during the Chola dynasty to create magnificent detailed metallic sculptures. 4. Architecture, Vāstu-Śāstra, and Town Planning Urban planning in India dates back to the Indus-Sarasvati Civilization (Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Dholavira), featuring gridiron street plans, standardized burnt brick dimensions (1:2:4 ratio), underground drainage networks, and sophisticated rainwater harvesting reservoirs. Classical architectural science is codified in Vāstu-śāstra treatises (such as Mānasāra, Mayamata, and Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra). Central to Vāstu design is the Vāstu-puruṣa-maṇḍala—a geometric grid (typically 8×8 or 9×9) that aligns built structures with natural cardinal directions, solar angles, and elemental forces.

Classical architectural science is codified in Vāstu-śāstra treatises (such as Mānasāra, Mayamata, and Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra). Central to Vāstu design is the Vāstu-puruṣa-maṇḍala—a geometric grid (typically 8×8 or 9×9) that aligns built structures with natural cardinal directions, solar angles, and elemental forces. Texts outline modular town layouts including Dandaka, Nandyāvarta, Sarvatobhadra, and Prastara patterns. Part 4: Humanities, Social Sciences & Governance 1. Ayurveda, Health, Wellness, and Psychology Ayurveda ('The Science of Life') defines health not merely as the absence of disease, but as a balanced state of physical energies, metabolic fire, bodily tissues, waste elimination, and mental/spiritual tranquility (Prasannātmentriyamanaḥ). Core physiological concepts include: • Tri-doṣa Framework: Vāta (air/space governing movement), Pitta (fire/water governing metabolism), and Kapha (water/earth governing structure). • Sapta-dhātu: Seven primary structural tissues—Rasa (plasma), Rakta (blood), Māṁsa (muscle), Medas (fat), Asthi (bone), Majjā (marrow), and Śukra (reproductive fluid). • Major Texts: Caraka-saṁhitā (internal medicine and diagnosis), Suśruta-saṁhitā (pioneering plastic surgery, rhinoplasty, and over 120 surgical instruments), and Aṣṭāṅga-hṛdaya. Indian psychology integrates the mind-body-consciousness complex across five layers (Pañca-koṣa): Annamaya (physical), Prāṇamaya (vital energy), Manomaya (mental/emotional), Vijñānamaya (intellectual), and Ānandamaya (blissful state). 2. Governance, Statecraft, and Public Administration Indian political philosophy provides sophisticated frameworks for state administration, economic prosperity (Artha), and societal order. Kautilya's Arthashastra (c. 4th century BCE) presents a comprehensive manual on statecraft, legal jurisprudence, treasury management, foreign policy, taxation, and intelligence networks. Central to Kautilya's state theory is the Saptāṅga Theory—the seven limbs of a state: 1. Swāmin (The Sovereign / King) 2. Amātya (Ministers and Officials) 3. Janapada (Territory and Population) 4. Durga (Fortified Capital) 5. Kośa (Treasury) 6. Daṇḍa / Bala (Military Forces) 7. Mitra (Allies and Foreign Relations)

Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.—At the commencement of this Constitution, every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and— (a) who was born in the territory of India; or (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or (c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India. 6.

Rights of citizenship of certain persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan.—Notwithstanding anything in article 5, a person who has migrated to the territory of India from the territory now included in Pakistan shall be deemed to be a citizen of India at the commencement of this Constitution if— (a) he or either of his parents or any of his grand-parents was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted); and (b)(i) in the case where such person has so migrated before the nineteenth day of July, 1948, he has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India since the date of his migration, or (ii) in the case where such person has so migrated on or after the nineteenth day of July, 1948, he has been registered as a citizen of India by an officer appointed in that behalf by the Government of the Dominion of India on an application made by him therefor to such officer before the commencement of this Constitution in the form and manner prescribed by that Government: Provided that no person shall be so registered unless he has been resident in the territory of India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of his application. 7. Rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan.— Notwithstanding anything in articles 5 and 6, a person who has after the first day of March, 1947, migrated from the territory of India to the territory now included in Pakistan shall not be deemed to be a citizen of India:

THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA (Part II.—Citizenship) Provided that nothing in this article shall apply to a person who, after having so migrated to the territory now included in Pakistan, has returned to the territory of India under a permit for resettlement or permanent return issued by or under the authority of any law and every such person shall for the purposes of clause (b) of article 6 be deemed to have migrated to the territory of India after the nineteenth day of July, 1948. 8. Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India.—Notwithstanding anything in article 5, any person who or either of whose parents or any of whose grand-parents was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted), and who is ordinarily residing in any country outside India as so defined shall be deemed to be a citizen of India if he has been registered as a citizen of India by the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where he is for the time being residing on an application made by him therefor to such diplomatic or consular representative, whether before or after the commencement of this Constitution, in the form and manner prescribed by the Government of the Dominion of India or the Government of India. 9. Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens.—No person shall be a citizen of India by virtue of article 5, or be deemed to be a citizen of India by virtue of article 6 or article 8, if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State. 10.

Continuance of the rights of citizenship.—Every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen of India under any of the foregoing provisions of this Part shall, subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament, continue to be such citizen. 11. Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.—Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship. PART III FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS General 12. Definition.—In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, “the State” includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. 13.

Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights.—(1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. (2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. (3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) “law” includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law; (b) “laws in force” includes laws passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that any such law or any part thereof may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas. 1[(4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368. Procedure for impeachment of the President.—(1) When a President is to be impeached for violation of the Constitution, the charge shall be preferred by either House of Parliament. (2) No such charge shall be preferred unless— (a) the proposal to prefer such charge is contained in a resolution which has been moved after at least fourteen days' notice in writing signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of the House has been given of their intention to move the resolution, and (b) such resolution has been passed by a majority of not less than twothirds of the total membership of the House. (3) When a charge has been so preferred by either House of Parliament, the other House shall investigate the charge or cause the charge to be investigated and the President shall have the right to appear and to be represented at such investigation. (4) If as a result of the investigation a resolution is passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House by which the charge was investigated or caused to be investigated, declaring that the charge preferred against the President has been sustained, such resolution shall have the effect of removing the President from his office as from the date on which the resolution is so passed. 62.

The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States.—(1) The Vice- President of India shall be ex officio Chairman of the Council of States. (2) The Council of States shall, as soon as may be, choose a member of the Council to be Deputy Chairman thereof and, so often as the office of Deputy Chairman becomes vacant, the Council shall choose another member to be Deputy Chairman thereof. 90.

Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman.—A member holding office as Deputy Chairman of the Council of States— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council: Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution. 91. Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman.—(1) While the office of Chairman is vacant, or during any period when the Vice-President is acting as, or discharging the functions of, President, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman, or, if the office of Deputy Chairman is also vacant, by such member of the Council of States as the President may appoint for the purpose. (2) During the absence of the Chairman from any sitting of the Council of States the Deputy Chairman, or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Council, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the Council, shall act as Chairman. 92.

The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration.—(1) At any sitting of the Council of States, while any resolution for the removal of the Vice- President from his office is under consideration, the Chairman, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Chairman, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 91 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Chairman, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Chairman, is absent. (2) The Chairman shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Council of States while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration in the Council, but, notwithstanding anything in article 100, shall not be entitled to vote at all on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings. 93. The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People.— The House of the People shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the House to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof and, so often as the office of Speaker or Deputy Speaker becomes vacant, the House shall choose another member to be Speaker or Deputy Speaker, as the case may be. 94.

Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker.— A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the House of the People; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Speaker, to the Deputy Speaker, and if such member is the Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then members of the House: Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution: Provided further that, whenever the House of the People is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution. 95.

Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker.—(1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker or, if the office of Deputy Speaker is also vacant, by such member of the House of the People as the President may appoint for the purpose. (2) During the absence of the Speaker from any sitting of the House of the People the Deputy Speaker or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the House, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the House, shall act as Speaker. 96.

96. The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration.—(1) At any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 95 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Speaker, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Speaker, is absent. (2) The Speaker shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the House of the People while any resolution for his removal from office is under consideration in the House and shall, notwithstanding anything in article 100, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings but not in the case of an equality of votes. 97. Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.—There shall be paid to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries and allowances as are specified in the Second Schedule. 98.

Secretariat of Parliament.—(1) Each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff: Provided that nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of Parliament. (2) Parliament may by law regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament. (3) Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (2), the President may, after consultation with the Speaker of the House of the People or the Chairman of the Council of States, as the case may be, make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of the House of the People or the Council of States, and any rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any law made under the said clause. Conduct of Business 99. Oath or affirmation by members.—Every member of either House of Parliament shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule. 100. Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum.—(1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of either House or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or person acting as Chairman or Speaker.

The Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes. (2) Either House of Parliament shall have power to act notwithstanding any vacancy in the membership thereof, and any proceedings in Parliament shall be valid notwithstanding that it is discovered subsequently that some person who was not entitled so to do sat or voted or otherwise took part in the proceedings. 1[(3) Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth of the total number of members of the House. (4) If at any time during a meeting of a House there is no quorum, it shall be the duty of the Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, either to adjourn the House or to suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.
